speakeroldname: Hon. David Crombie (Secretary of State of Canada):
speakerposition: Minister responsible for Multiculturalism; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise today to inform the House that the National Forum on Post-Secondary Education will be held in Saskatoon, Saskatchewan, from October 25 to October 28. The aim of the forum will be to explore the challenges and opportunities facing Canada's universities and colleges in preparation for the 1990s and the 21st century. Learning is a lifelong process and our institutions must become flexible enough to respond to the differing needs of the 45-year old executive, the 65-year old pensioner, and the 18-year old student fresh from high school. These are formidable challenges and demand the utmost from all involved in postsecondary education.

This Forum will not be a federal event, a provincial event, or even a federal-provincial event. It will be an historic occasion for discussion among informed and concerned Canadians. The role of the governments here is to facilitate such discussions and respond to the issues and concerns that are raised.

The planning of the forum will be in the hands of a national committee, a group of eminent and respected Canadians from across the country. I am pleased to announce today, together with the Chairman of the Council of Ministers of Education, the Hon. Anthony Brummet, the names of those who will be responsible for organizing the event.
Chairing the National Forum Committee will be Dr. Brian Segal, President of Ryerson Polytechnical Institute. He will be supported by two vice-chairpersons: Dr. Jean-Guy Paquet, Rector of Laval University; and Dr. Sylvia Fedoruk, Chancellor of the University of Saskatchewan. The remaining persons on the steering committee include: Jill Bodkin, Chairman, British Columbia Securities Commission; Adrienne Clarkson, President and Publisher of McClelland and Stewart Publishers; John Evans, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer of Allelix Incorporated; Paul Gallagher, President of Vancouver Community College; Claude Pichette, President, Societe d'entraide economique du Quebec, the Hon. Robert L. Stanfield, Chairman, Institute for Research on Public Policy; Genevieve Tanguay, student at Laval University; Ronald Watts, Professor, Political Science, Queen's University; Noel Stoodley, the Canadian Labour Congress.

The complete list of members of the National Forum Committee, which we are releasing today, includes Canadians from all walks of life: students, teachers and administrators from the academic community, and representatives of business, labour, and other interested groups.

It may well be advisable that I read the list of those who are going to participate because it shows the breadth, depth, and importance of this National Forum. They include: Lise Bisson-nette, journalist, Quebec City; Gina Blondin, school teacher and graduate student, University of British Columbia, from the Northwest Territories; Paul Davenport, Vice-Principal, Planning and Computer Services, McGill University; Ronald Duhamel, Professor of Educational Administration, University of Manitoba, Winnipeg; William Dunbar, Vice-President and General Manager, NorthwesTel; Gilbert Finn, Chairman of the Board and Chief Executive Officer, Assumption Mutual Life Insurance Company, Moncton; Graham Flack, student, Dalhousie University, Halifax; Paul Gallagher, President, Vancouver Community College; Therese Gouin-Decarie, Professor of Psychology, University of Montreal, Montreal; Ray Hainsworth, Comptroller, Ontario Workers' Occupational and Safety Health Centre; Paul Inchauspe, Director General,

March 30, 1987
Statements by Ministers
CEGEP Ahuntsic; Linda Inkpen, member of the Board of Directors of the Cabot Institute in St. John's, Newfoundland; Anthony Johnstone, Executive Director, Nova Scotia Human Rights Commission; Gordin Kaplan, Professor of Biochemistry and Vice-President, Research, University of Alberta; Muriel Kovitz, Chancellor, University of Calgary; Ian MacDonald, Director of Extension and Summer School, University of Prince Edward Island, Charlottetown; Tony Macerollo, Chairman, Canadian Federation of Students, Ottawa; Andrew MacKay, Ombudsman, Province of Nova Scotia; Colin MacKay, former President, University of New Brunswick; John Panabaker, Chairman, Mutual Life of Canada, Waterloo; Charles Pascal, President, Sir Stanford Fleming Community College, Peterborough; Frank Smith, Co-ordinator, National Educational Association of Disabled Students, Ottawa; Ahab Spence, Teacher of Cree and Indian Studies, University of Regina; John Stoik, former Chief Executive Officer, Gulf Oil Canada, Saskatchewan; David Strangway, President, University of British Columbia, Vancouver; Edward K. Turner, Executive Director, Prairie Pools Inc., Saskatchewan Wheat Pool, Regina; Dorothy Wills, teacher, Vanier College; and Claudia Wright, Associate Professor of Political Science, University of Winnipeg.
[DOT] (mo)
I read the entire list because it is important that people understand the representativeness and excellence of the group which will carry on the National Forum.
Members of the House will recall that in the Speech from the Throne last October the Government reaffirmed its commitment to supporting, with the provinces, a system of post-secondary education based on excellence and equality of opportunity. At that time we proposed that a national forum on post-secondary education would be convened to provide the opportunity for a full discussion of the challenges and opportunities facing our colleges and universities as we approach the 21st century.

Following the speech from the Throne, I undertook extensive consultations. In particular, I met individually with most provincial Ministers responsible for post-secondary education and, on February 2, I met with the full Council of Ministers of Education.

Everywhere I went I discovered widespread support for the forum and I was particularly pleased that the Council of Ministers of Education agreed to co-sponsor the event. I have also received numerous letters of support for the forum and expressions of interest from individuals and groups right across the country. Everyone wants to avoid the forum being simply a replay of some of the sterile debates we have had in this country about the specifics of post-secondary education financing arrangements. The forum is a much-needed opportunity for dialogue and co-operation among all sectors of our
society; government, business, scientists, educators and young people.

I see the forum also as an occasion for the federal Government to show leadership in the critical area of higher education and university research. I don't mean a leadership based on control and supervision-which inevitably leads to confrontation and discord-but one which was defined so well by the Honourable Claude Ryan in a 1984 conference on federal-provincial issues; "A leadership of inspiration, encouragement, and support."

The forum will enable us to look to the future with a broader vision, to examine the issues and opportunities facing our universities and colleges, and to help make us ready for the challenges of the next century.
To quote the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) in a recent address to the University of Waterloo on the topic of research and development;
The western world is moving toward knowledge-based economics, and Canada must move with it. We want to be known not only as a resource-rich nation, not only as a trading nation, but as a nation known for our brainpower, our ideas, and our intellectual and educational achievements. The issue is no less fundamental than how Canada will earn a living in the 1990s and beyond



The forum will help all Canadians appreciate the challenges facing our post-secondary system in the years ahead. We now have the organizational framework for the forum in place.

I am confident that the co-operative approach we have established will produce a very successful event and contribute to making our post-secondary education system one of the best in the world.
Hear, hear!

speakeroldname: Hon. William Rompkey (Grand Falls-White Bay- Labrador):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to thank the Minister for sending me a copy of his statement in advance. Along with all Hon. Members and all Canadians, I am pleased that this forum is going ahead about a year after it was mentioned in the Throne Speech. I believe that the Minister has put together a blue-ribbon steering committee. There is some balance on that committee, certainly in the male-female ratio, but I would point out to him the absence on the steering committee of a member of the Canadian Federation of Students. The President is on the committee, but not on the steering committee. Students, whose fate is most involved and whose future is most at risk, should be on the steering committee itself rather than only on the committee. I make that suggestion to the Minister.
The Minister said in his statement that he wants a positive, wide-ranging and national dialogue rather than only a federal-provincial dialogue. I think that is important. He also said that he does not want a repeat of the sterile debate on financing.
March 30, 1987

However, that is surely fundamental to a healthy system of post-secondary education. Apropos of that, I want to draw to his attention an article from The Sunday Express from Newfoundland this weekend which draws attention very graphically to a real crisis in post-secondary education. The headline reads, "Memorial University in Crisis". The article reads:
Mortar is oozing out from between the bricks on several buildings around campus. Buckets catch water dripping in an underground tunnel system that is not properly maintained. Department heads this year requested $4.2 million in funding for 125 teaching positions. Of the 125, zero was authorized.
I could go on. The President of the University did not want to go public but was forced to talk about a real crisis in postsecondary education with regard to the maintenance of buildings, the number of students, and the kind of support they are getting.
I would like to draw to the attention of the Minister two other events which show that this problem is not confined to Atlantic Canada. The University of Regina was told on the weekend that it was receiving a zero per cent increase in funding this year and that it has to retire its deficit of $6 million over the next four years. At Carleton University a referendum is taking place today on whether there should be a $15 increase in the annual student fees from now on to provide for the construction of buildings and repairs to the campus. Carleton University is not one of the poorest universities in a province which is not one of the poorest in the country.
I believe that these examples illustrate graphically that there is a serious crisis all across the country, not only in national policy but indeed in funding. We can construct a vehicle, but if we do not have gas in the tank of the vehicle it will not go anywhere. EPF and Canada student loans must be on the agenda for that forum.
It is important that we have this debate at the same time as the child care issue and proposals for it are coming forward. Women are the most disadvantaged in the country in terms of access to post-secondary education. We recognize that child care is important as well and we will have a debate on that issue. However, if women are really going to achieve equality it is important to have access to improved education. That is fundamental to the achievement of equality for women. That should be highlighted at this discussion in the forum on postsecondary education. Women must be involved and their particular case must be put forward.
I do not want to give the impression that I feel negatively in any way about this forum because I think it is a good initiative, one which we have called for for the past two years. However, I want to ask what the follow-up to this forum will be. That is very important. We can have a three-day forum of learned discussion as the beginning of a national debate on post-secondary education, but it is what happens the day after which is important. I hope the Minister can give a commitment that after that forum the Government will listen and seriously consider the recommendations of that forum and make a commitment to follow up. I would like to hear the
Statements by Ministers
Minister say he is hopeful about establishing an ongoing permanent national advisory council on post-secondary education.
A three-day forum will not be enough. Canadians must build on that three-day forum and indeed create a policy that is not federal or provincial, but a national policy on postsecondary education. Such a policy requires continuous administration.
I welcome the leadership the Minister is showing this morning and the fact that he has also brought the provinces into this initiative. Indeed, I believe some provinces, such as Quebec and Ontario, have shown leadership themselves. Ontario has shown leadership recently with its announcement of an increase in funding and its initiatives toward postsecondary education. The Minister will know that many other provinces still have much to do in order to have a total consensus about what must be done in post-secondary education in this country.
Therefore, while I welcome the announcement today, I want to repeat those three points. First, students must be involved at the top level in planning for this forum; second, the agenda must include the funding of post-secondary education in the future; and third, there must a commitment to follow up.

Mr. Speaker, the university system is in crisis, just as science, research and technology has been in crisis for the last several years. The Government has done very little in either area.
When faced with the crisis of a deterioration in research, science and technology and innovation, the Government held a forum. The appropriate reaction was that at least it is doing something, however little. Now, we will have a forum on postsecondary education. Again, the appropriate response is that at least the Government is doing something.
When faced with concern about the post-secondary educational system and education in general in the United States, the President formed a commission and the Carnegie Foundation conducted an investigation which led to considerable reform and increased financing in many states in the U.S. But we will have a forum.
Many of the provinces have conducted Royal commissions on post-secondary education, all of which have identified a deterioration in the state of our universities in many provinces and stated that reform was necessary if the system was not to deteriorate to the point where it would serve no national or provincial purpose. But we will have a forum.
Leaders in industry, academia, and students all across this land have sounded the cry of alarm about the failure of governments, both provincial and federal, to recognize the importance of the university for our future economic development and opportunities for our youth. But the federal Government is going to have a forum.

March 30, 1987
Committee Reports
Everyone who is interested in universities has condemned the federal Government for cutting back on the rate of increase in transfer payments for the funding of universities. They have indicated that there clearly is an urgent need for the federal and provincial Governments to get together and to establish their respective responsibilities toward post-secondary education. The need is clear, but the federal Government is going to have a forum.
Many of us have said that an advisory council on postsecondary education must be established. Indeed, such a council should engage in a long-term and continuing study of elementary and secondary education. It must study the needs of post-secondary education and elaborate on the kind of policy that the OECD indicates this country needs desperately. But the Government is going to have a forum and solve all of these problems in three days.
The Canadian Association of University Teachers, the Association of Universities and Colleges of Canada, and the Canadian Federation of Students and many of those who are interested in post-secondary education and research and science have had repeated forums. They may even welcome another forum as a result of their experience.
A few months ago there was a forum on science, research and technology that was held in Winnipeg. There were five recommendations as a result of that forum, but no action.
Louder.
You think it is funny over there.

One cannot speak loud enough to call attention to the utter failure of the Government to respond to the needs of youth and all those who ought to be served by post-secondary education in this country. I will congratulate the Government for holding a forum and at least doing one thing right. Indeed, it has invited representative groups of Canadians to participate in the forum and I give the Government credit for ensuring that there is some degree of representation of women, visible minorities, natives, youth and others.
While that is good, the need has been demonstrated so clearly that the Government should be able to see beyond another forum. Yet there will be another three days of talking about post-secondary education while we wait for the Minister of State for Youth (Mr. Charest) to produce his policy for youth. Part of that policy should include action on the restrictions to accessibility and opportunity in post-secondary institutions in this country. But we will have another forum.
I hope it is a good forum. I hope the Government will listen to what it has been told repeatedly, that it has responsibility for exercising leadership, for full participation in the funding of post-secondary education, and a responsibility to find a solution to the impasse between the federal and provincial levels so there will be a stable level of financing for postsecondary institutions. Perhaps it will realize that it is time to stop having forums and will direct its attention toward
implementing a national advisory council on post-secondary education.
It is interesting to note that the Secretary of State (Mr. Crombie) mentioned the need for increased attention to research in universities and elsewhere. I hope the Government will stop closing laboratories, transferring scientists and playing games with the scientific community, that it will stop holding forums and make a determined effort to improve the situation in this country with respect to science, research and technology.
While we do not need any more forums, the Government may need them because it has failed to appreciate the dimensions of the problem or recognize the solutions to it.

subtopic: PRESENTATION OF FINAL REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
PRESENTATION OF FINAL REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have the honour to present the final report of the Special Committee on Child Care in both official languages.
It is with great pleasure that I table the report. It represents 15 months of exceptional effort by members of all Parties. It is a report which I believe reflects the views of most Canadian families. It is a report that challenges the Government and its provincial and territorial counterparts, that challenges the child care system, volunteer organizations and, most important, Canadian families. It is a report which offers no simple solutions. It recognizes that no one approach can effectively deal with the unique and diverse needs of Canadians. With this in mind, it is important that the recommendations put forward by this committee be examined as a complete package rather than isolated components.
This report opens many doors. It is now up to all of us to ensure that Canadian children receive the love, encouragement and quality care they so richly deserve.
I would also indicate that the committee, in accordance with Standing Order 99 (2) requests that the Government table a comprehensive report to its recommendations.

speakeroldname: Hon. Flora MacDonald (for the Minister of State (Privatization)) moved
subtopic: TELEGLOBE CANADA REORGANIZATION AND DIVESTITURE ACT
speechtext: that Bill C-38, an Act respecting the reorganization and divestiture of Teleglobe Canada, be read the third time and passed.

subtopic: TELEGLOBE CANADA REORGANIZATION AND DIVESTITURE ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would just like to say a few words on this particular Bill at third reading. Perhaps the question should be asked at third reading why the Government of Canada is selling Teleglobe. Why did it decide to sell Teleglobe at this time? Why did it decide to sell Teleglobe, period? Was there any great reason for its sale? Was it a philosophical reason? Was it a financial reason? Was it that it was competing with private enterprise? As I understand it, the answer to those questions from members of the Government is yes.
March 30, 1987

We are dealing here with a company that actually makes money. It makes incredible profits. One would suspect that when a company makes money and is a monopoly, as has been pointed out by members of the Government, that one would use a bit of arithmetic to try to figure out what such a company is worth to the Canadian taxpayer. Would you, Mr. Speaker, sell for $400 million a company that makes $100 million a year and has a monopoly?

subtopic: TELEGLOBE CANADA REORGANIZATION AND DIVESTITURE ACT
speechtext: Why not?

subtopic: TELEGLOBE CANADA REORGANIZATION AND DIVESTITURE ACT
speechtext:
An Hon. Member sitting on the government benches asks "Why not?" This is a member of the Progressive Conservative Party saying "Why not?" Why not sell a company that makes $100 million for $400 million? That seems to be the financial philosophy of this Government. In other words, for a short term gain before March 31 to deal with the deficit-not the national debt but the deficit-the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) says: "Would it not be lovely to have another $500 million knocked off the deficit for the financial year before we reach March 31?" That is the financial philosophy of the Government of Canada today. It goes from March 31 to March 31 to March 31. There is always a scramble at the end trying to figure out how the deficit can be reduced by x number of dollars. Why? So that it can carry through with the philosophy it espoused during the election campaign.
Where has this philosophy gotten the Government of Canada? When one looks at the national debt of the country one discovers that in the short time that this Government has been in power the debt has climbed more than in any other time in our history. There is no other three-year period in our history in which we can find that the national debt rose at the rate which it has risen under the present Government. It is the highest rise in the national debt, the entire national debt of Canada, that we have ever seen. This includes the accumulated deficits of every Government since Confederation.
The Minister of Finance says that the national debt has risen by one-third since his Government took power. The accumulated deficit since Confederation has risen by 30 per cent since the Government came to power. Why is that? The Government's usual response is that it is because of the previous administration. That is the reason which is always given. The first year in which the Government was in office the deficit was about $37 billion or $38 billion. Members of the Government said that that was due to the previous administration. The next year came along and what was the deficit then? It was about $35 billion, give or take $3 billion or $4 billion. I am not sure of the exact figure. At any rate, members of the Government said it was due to the previous administration. They projected that the deficit would go below $30 billion in the next year. If we look at the publications of the Minister of Finance, including his budget projections and fiscal plans, we see that for two years in a row it was projected that the deficit would go down below $30 billion. What happened after that?
Teleglobe Canada
In the next Budget the Government said it had missed the mark by $4 billion or $5 billion. Members of the Government said, "We are now projecting that it will go down to under $30 billion in the next year". However, next year will come along and they will say, "We were off $4 billion or $5 billion in our projections because of this, that or the other thing, but next year it will go down to less than $30 billion".
There has never been a time in Canadian financial history in which we have had such a disastrous record as far as the deficit is concerned. Yet the Government claims that it is selling Crown corporations because it wants to reduce the deficit and the national debt. Mr. Speaker, I am sure you can recall all the Bills that went through this Chamber in a hurry giving $1 billion here and $1 billion there. Do you remember, Mr. Speaker, when the Government gave $1 billion here and there to foreign banks? Do Hon. Members remember that? Do Hon. Members remember when the Government gave money to rich people, the millionaires, buddies of the Government and friends of cabinet Ministers? Do Hon. Members remember when the banks were bailed out? It did not make much difference at that time that $1 billion was being handed out here and there. Nor did it make much difference at certain other times when there was a real reason for granting such sums of money.
Why then does the Government of Canada come along all of a sudden and say, it is going to sell Teleglobe? I would say that 99 per cent of the people in Canada do not even know what Teleglobe is. Why should they? It is a Crown corporation that handles telecommunications. It does not actually charge for it, it just handles telecommunications, mostly across the Atlantic Ocean. This is a marvellous company which gave the Government of Canada $108.1 million last year and another $80 million this year. Of course, the Government of Canada is now saying that it is up for sale and, in fact, it will sell this company to another company called Memotec, which I believe is the name of the company. At any rate, the chairman of the board is a fellow by the name of Baker. The Government now wishes to sell the company for a song. It will make Memotec the prize of the stock market, just as Fishery Products International was made the prize of the stock market. The same is true with respect to other sales that the Minister responsible has carried out and is carrying out at the present time.
We can see on the face of it that it is difficult to try to figure out why the Government is selling Teleglobe. It is very difficult to figure it out. One could stretch it on this or that point, but one would come to the end and say, there is no reason whatsoever for the Government to sell Teleglobe. I am now searching for reasons for this sale. speechtext:
The former Minister just said "by us"; and "by us", he means, of course, the Liberal Government of the day.
FPI was set up at a time when fish plants were closing all over eastern Canada, with hundreds and thousands of people being laid off. This was something that was being done by a very large private sector company at a time when fish prices had gone down. The whole of the fisheries industry at the time
was in financial trouble. The Government of Canada created a Crown corporation, and it did so because that was the only way to go. Both the federal and provincial governments jointly took the decision to create a Crown corporation, and that is exactly what they did.
Fishery Products International was created to save jobs, to save the industry, and to maintain continuity insofar as the export of Canada's fisheries products was concerned. One does not want to see, in terms of international markets, a substantial drop in the export of any one commodity, as another country will then come along to fill that vacuum. Once the industry recovers and plants are reopened, it is difficult to regain lost markets. For that reason, it was important that the Government of Canada act very swiftly to maintain the supply of Canada's fisheries products into the international markets. Insofar as the nation's economy was concerned, and the economies of the affected provinces, not to mention the thousands of jobs affected by a substantial downturn in prices, there was good reason for the creation of FPI.
The world has now changed insofar as fisheries products are concerned. Current demand is high in all parts of the world. There are many fisheries products in the market-place-frozen fish products, fresh fish products, fish fillets, and so forth. In certain instances, fisheries products are almost refined products. With the supply remaining relatively the same, with the increased demand, we have had increased prices.
What we have seen, Mr. Speaker, in FPI, a Crown corporation that controlled 30 to 35 individual companies in eastern Canada, is a substantial increase in the bottom line. Substantial profits have been made. I believe last year the profit was something in the order of $24 million to $30 million. This represents quite a turn around insofar as the fisheries industry is concerned. FPI was a Crown corporation owned by the federal and provincial governments.
This Government then decided to get rid of that Crown corporation. Given that FPI no longer fulfilled a public purpose, one can understand the sale of FPI. There was a guarantee in the sale that the employees would be taken care of, that the employees would not lose their pension contributions, and that they would maintain their positions in the workforce. There was a also a condition of sale whereby if for any reason the new board of this now private sector corporation decided that any one of the individual operations was to be closed down or sold, the Government of Canada and the affected provincial Government would be notified and given the first option to purchase.
The FPI sales agreement was drawn and supervised by some very prominent Newfoundlanders, and we have in the telecommunications industry in this country today some very prominent Newfoundlanders. When those individuals drew up the sales agreement in respect of Fishery Products International they left no holes. No employee could turn around and accuse the Government of Canada of not taking care of jobs, of not ensuring that each community was protected. The Government of Canada ensured, through the sales agreement, that the new
March 30, 1987

board of directors, the new shareholders of that company, understood that they could not close any individual plant connected with that former Crown corporation without making a first offer to the Government.
Why is it, Mr. Speaker, that the Minister who handled the FPI sale so well now comes before the House with this measure? In the one case, the Minister came into the House and read out a glorious statement in respect of the sale of Fishery Products International. In the case of the sale of FPI, we had an agreement with all of the guarantees written in, an agreement with not even a shadow of a doubt that the employees would not be taken care of. In fact, we had the Government even instructing the new owners that they could not sell a portion of the business at any time without first giving the Government of Canada and the affected provincial Government the first option of purchase, and the same guarantee applied to plant closures.
Everybody appeared to be quite happy with that agreement. The Minister made the announcement, and the shares of FPI were listed for sale on the stock market, and were immediately bought up by investors.
The value of the shares was nine to one as far as the profits were concerned. The Government gave factory freezer trawlers to another profitable company called National Sea Products and gave them permission to operate it in eastern Canada, against the wishes of fishermen. As I say, the company was very profitable in the fish business.
The Minister made a statement in the House of Commons assuring the employees of their guaranteed benefits, saying that the new owners of the company would have to abide by the rules. After saying that they were not allowed to touch a piece of equipment in all the plants in eastern Canada, unless they notified the federal Government, what did the Minister do? The Minister of State for Privatization (Mrs. McDougall) will be sending out a letter today to all Teleglobe employees. Actually, the letter is dated March 27, 1987, but it will be going out today. It is a four-page letter. I do not want to get into its particulars, but it goes back to a problem which the Government brought on itself in the clause in the Bill dealing with employees and their pensions.
I would like to read into the record a letter from the Teleglobe Canada Ad Hoc Committee on Pensions. It is signed by Mr. Carlos Saldanha and Mr. E. A. Rutherford, Ted Rutherford, who are in charge of the committee. The letter was sent to the Minister of State for Privatization and Minister responsible for regulatory affairs. In part it reads:
We, the Teleglobe Ad Hoc Pension Committee, understand that it is in the
best interest of the parties concerned that Bill C-38 be passed and come into
effect by March 31, 1987. We also wish to see this date achieved.
If that were not in the letter, I guarantee that the Bill would not be passed through the House before March 31. It would not be passed in the House unless the pension committee wished it to be passed.
Teleglobe Canada
I cannot see any other reason for passing the Bill other than standing up and protecting Teleglobe employees. They might change their minds if the Minister does not answer their letter properly. However, it goes on to say:
However, some issues related to transferring values for past service, in our opinion, are still not resolved.
We are getting to the pension issue now. It continues:
We expect that your Government will endeavour to sit down with representatives of this committee, as was previously promised by the Honourable Robert de Cotret, to reach an equitable solution in the process of developing a Reciprocal Transfer Agreement.
We all know what reciprocal transfer agreements are as far as pensions are concerned. Then it continues:
A proper transfer agreement, when coupled with the future plan offered by Memotec,-
That is the name of the company which is buying Teleglobe for a song. It continues:
-which we note was more generous than the norm your Government recommended, will maintain Teleglobe's pension plan features for existing employees as they were prior to privatization.
In other words, at the last minute, at the last hour, members of the ad hoc committee on pensions are saying to Members of the House of Commons, "Let us help the Government get the Bill through before March 31". However, they are also saying that they need a reciprocal transfer agreement on their pensions.
I looked at the letter from the Minister which will go out today to all Teleglobe employees. I looked for some substance in it. Before the day is out, perhaps the Minister will be able to explain to the House what the particular letter means. However, we know what the reciprocal transfer agreement is all about.
You and I, Mr. Speaker, know what happens when someone changes employment. For example, when workers are laid off from a Crown corporation, are given early retirement, or whatever the case may be, they always hope and pray for a reciprocal transfer agreement on their pensions. Why is that? It is because they are interested in adding the time they were employed somewhere else on to their new employment. When a lay-off or an early retirement takes place in a Crown corporation, the man who is affected always looks back at where he worked 10 years ago, 20 years ago, or 30 years ago. Perhaps he worked with the department of highways in a provincial Government or something like that. Then he wonders whether he can transfer his pension benefits from the provincial government department to the Crown corporation and add it all together. Perhaps he will wonder if the private company for which he might work will take his accumulated pension benefits from years of service into its pension scheme and honour them.
There are people in Canada today who make a living in Crown corporations examining whether it is to their benefit to have reciprocal transfer agreements or pension transfer agreements. I imagine that the office of Canadian National in Montreal would have people working on that continually.

March 30, 1987
Tele globe Canada
It is interesting to note that a Government which wanted to get rid of Crown corporations and said that they were a menace to society would create a Crown corporation to save money, that is, Marine Atlantic. That Crown corporation has a pension transfer agreement with the Province of New Brunswick, the Province of Prince Edward Island, and the Province of Quebec. However, it does not have one with the Province of Nova Scotia or with the Province of Newfoundland. It is amazing that a Crown corporation would be laying off people or offering them early retirement at this time of the year and have no signed pension transfer agreement.
Employees of Teleglobe are interested in a reciprocal transfer agreement as it relates to their pension funds. The Government of Canada through the Treasury Board should have had this worked out some time ago. It should have made sure that this issue would not arise during the final moments of the sale of the Crown corporation, but it did not do so. The Government did not satisfy the employees of Teleglobe otherwise the employees would not have written such a letter dated March 27, 1987. Why is the Government of Canada selling Teleglobe today? Why did the Government sell another Crown corporation at the same time it created another one? I suggest it was to save money? The whole thing does not add up, Mr. Speaker.
In the letter being sent by the Minister of State for Privatization, certain blanket guarantees are supposed to be made to the employees of Teleglobe. I think what would be of benefit in the Chamber today is to have a statement directly from the Minister or the Parliamentary Secretary to the effect that they will comply with the wishes of the Teleglobe Canada ad hoc committee on pensions, that they will immediately sit down with them and immediately state publicly in the House of Commons before the Bill is passed today exactly what the Government of Canada has in mind for all the employees. It is a very confusing scenario. It is not clear at all what the Government of Canada has in mind.
This Crown corporation, as we know, has to do with telecommunications. It is the carrier of the telephone lines, the telegraph lines and the telex lines from Canada to other countries in the world. It is the sole carrier. It is the actual carrier of the message. It is a guaranteed monopoly for the next five years which is being put under a regulatory agency, I believe the CRTC. Under those circumstances, with the incredible investment made at the beginning in Teleglobe, with the incredible amounts of money used to build cables across the Atlantic and at the same time to have the satellite feed in case the cable breaks-if the cable breaks, then the satellite is there, and if something goes wrong with the satellite, the cable is there-for this company now to be getting into the business of new cables, into fibreoptics and everything else at a cost of probably hundreds of millions of dollars or even billions of dollars, $400 million or $500 million seems a very small price to pay to purchase such an operation.
One wonders about the philosophy of the actual sale of Teleglobe and the recommendations of the Government of Canada respecting Crown corporations. What about the Government being involved in businesses that perhaps should be in the realm of the private sector? Will the overriding philosophy of the Government of Canada be, let's get rid of everything that we believe the private sector can do? If the private sector cannot possibly fulfil a transportation function in Canada, then we will maintain our presence. Yet even in that area today we hear the Government of Canada saying to Crown corporations "Cut, cut, cut. Reduce, reduce, reduce." What was the message with Teleglobe? Efficiency exports came into the shops of Teleglobe and said, "Let's cut here, there and some place else". The same thing has happened to practically every other corporation in Canada today, especially in the telecommunications business. We have several Crown corporations in the telecommunications business.

It is unfortunate that we do not have more competition in the telecommunications field. It is unfortunate that a monopoly exists. Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to take part in the third reading debate on Bill C-38. I will be speaking specifically to the Bill and the divestiture of Teleglobe rather than giving a long dissertation about everything under the sun in order to pass the time. We have just been given a little education on supply and demand economics and almost how fish patties are made. I was surprised to hear a whole speech built around why the employees do not want the Bill passed when the Hon. Member has a letter in his hands from the employees who appear to be pleading to have the Bill passed. I think they understand that they can best handle the negotiations for the proper transfer of pension benefits.
The sale of Teleglobe is an important initiative by this Government. The legislative and policy initiatives associated with it are designed to protect the interests of consumers and employees, and provide for regulation of the privatized company in order to ensure that Canada's international obligations continue to be met and provide Teleglobe with the opportunity to pursue a bright and exciting future.
I want to express my appreciation and that of the Minister to members of the committee for their conscientious review of the legislation. We also should say thank you to the witnesses for their valuable assistance in committee. Certainly I am delighted that a frank and full debate has taken place and that the many interested parties have had an opportunity for a balanced discussion, to the greatest extent possible.
Since the legislative review process began a few weeks ago certain amendments were made in the committee and I would like to briefly explain them for the benefit of Hon. Members. First, discussions with employee representatives led the

March 30, 1987
Teleglobe Canada
committee to conclude that an amendment to the Bill would add greater certainty to the pension alternatives available to those employees. Accordingly, an amendment was made to delete Clause 24(l)(b) in its entirety. Second, there was a series of minor technical changes made in committee to improve or clarify the language of the Bill. There was a minor change to Clause 4(3) to make the language consistent with similar clauses such as Clause 19. There were changes to the wording of Clause 5 but no change to the spirit of the provision. It was to improve or clarify the clause as it relates to the associate rules. There were a few phrases in Clause 5, Clause 13 and Clause 18 where the French and English versions differed as to meaning. Changes were made to rectify that situation. In order to facilitate the creation of a new corporate entity with the name Teleglobe Canada and avoid any possible confusion it was appropriate to change the name of the old company while its affairs were being wound up, and a new Clause 20 was added while Clause 21 was amended accordingly. This amendment also necessitated appropriate renumbering changes and the reference to clause numbers in Clause 34 as well as the addition of the new name in Schedule II.
I believe all Hon. Members would agree that the Government has been forthcoming in terms of the information it has made available in connection with this transaction. We provided extensive documentation and offered technical briefings to assist Hon. Members in their understanding of the sale of Teleglobe to Memotec. This is indeed a complicated transaction. By appreciating the many benefits of this privatization I am sure Hon. Members will understand the advantages to both consumers and Teleglobe employees and to the telecommunications industry itself. The timely passage of Bill C-38 is important.
Opportunities for growth and employment have been foremost in our objectives for this privatization. This Bill will sanction the alliance between Teleglobe and Memotec, thus creating a dynamic new force in the Canadian telecommunications industry. Teleglobe's proven technical expertise and industry experience will get renewed vigour from Memotec's entrepreneurial energy and marketing abilities. I will give you a few examples of the kinds of benefits that will be in store for Canada once this sale is completed.
While Teleglobe has profited under good management, it still had to perform under the operational restrictions of Crown ownership. Expansion was pre-empted because of impediments imposed on Teleglobe as a result of legislators and bureaucratic requirements. Consequently, Teleglobe was kept from exploring other avenues of growth despite its recognized industry expertise.
However, Memotec can give to Teleglobe what Crown ownership could not, the freedom to grow, expand and mature. Memotec understands the dynamics and the opportunities of the telecommunications market-place. It has proven itself as a force to contend with in the business world by its marketing,
sales and distribution expertise. In addition to Teleglobe's client base, Memotec will add its own international market base and its own customer network which includes major corporations in banking, insurance, transportation, other governments and so on.
A new Teleglobe allied with Memotec can create and take advantage of opportunities presented by this added national and international market base. The word "synergy", which has been coined of late, describes this kind of alliance. In simple terms this means the creation of new products and services offered in expanded markets and generous new exports. Such dynamic growth potential will create more opportunities for Canadians in all parts of the country.
Private ownership under public regulation will continue to serve the public interest while providing further benefits to consumers. Effective January 1, 1988, there will be a rate reduction on overseas telephone calls of more than 13 per cent. In addition, telex rates will decrease by 10 per cent at the same time. Consumers will also benefit from special protection of their telecommunications services through CRTC regulation. This is a new safeguard which was not present under Crown ownership. Thus, lower rates will be charged for the same high standard of services to which all Canadians have become accustomed. Consumers will benefit over-all, either by taking advantage of savings or by using services more frequently or for a longer duration.
I am especially pleased with the care that was taken by the Government to ensure that employees' interests were safeguarded. It was clear in the Government's announcement of November 19 that employee concerns were a key factor in setting the terms and conditions under which Teleglobe would be sold. I and my colleagues in the Government were sensitive to employees from the very beginning of the privatization process of Teleglobe. The Minister personally met with employee representatives prior to the initiation of the final round of bidding. Meetings were held over the course of the last few months between officials and Teleglobe employee representatives where employee concerns, particularly related to the future pension arrangements, were given ample discussion. In recognition of these concerns, Memotec's generous employee package was a key factor in supporting the Government decision to select this firm as the preferred purchaser for Teleglobe.
I think all Members must agree that Teleglobe employees are being well taken care of. For example, Teleglobe employees will remain under federal labour jurisdiction and all existing collective agreements will remain in force. As compared to industry norm, Memotec has offered a generous pension proposal, a plan which will be equivalent to the federal public service pension plan for all existing employees of Teleglobe. Furthermore, I would like to point out that we took heed of employees' interest in purchasing shares of Teleglobe. This was proposed by representatives of employees crossing all union lines. They had a very special interest in purchasing, and
March 30, 1987

a purchase arrangement is therefore included in the agreement. Special provision has been made for an employee share ownership program which will offer 5 per cent of shares to employees at a discount of 10 per cent with interest-free loans available from the company.
In addition, Memotec has undertaken to make every effort to qualify employee share purchases under the Quebec stock savings plan and similar plans implemented by other provinces. Finally, in order to limit the disruption to employees and management, the legislation provides that Teleglobe's headquarters will remain in Montreal.
The discussion with regard to pensions centred on the transfer of past service. I asked a Treasury Board official what transfer of past service he would receive if he went to work at a university as compared to what employees would receive under this plan. This plan is substantially better than the benefits available to a federal employee who goes to work for one of our universities.
It seems that the question of whether the Government is receiving fair value for Teleglobe has finally been put to rest. At committee even the Hon. Member for Essex-Windsor (Mr. Langdon) recognized that a reasonably good price had been received for the company. However, for the record, I want to state that Memotec is paying the Government $488.3 million which is a premium of $110 million over the revised book value of $378 million. I believe this represents a very good return for the taxpayers' investment in Teleglobe. Added to that, of course, were profits of over $100 million plus another $18 million.
You can see, Mr. Speaker, that the sale of Teleglobe to Memotec is a good deal for all interested parties. An equal and fair balance has been struck for taxpayers, shareholders, customers and, very importantly, the employees. The result will be a more dynamic and exciting new Teleglobe with advantages for all Canadians and for the telecommunications industry.
The passing of Bill C-38 will make Teleglobe our eleventh privatization since the Government came into power. This is a forward-looking program based upon a vision the Government has developed to promote better management of public resources and to create new opportunities in industry. I have only to point out the success of de Havilland and Canadair. I noticed that the previous speaker never referred to the additional employees and the additional business which has been generated at de Havilland and the positive environment of Canadair. Our vision has created more flexibility, new challenges and greater incentives for these firms and their employees to pursue new opportunities for growth. In following this course we have prepared these companies for the future rather than anchoring them in the past.
Teleglobe Canada
The rapid pace of technological advances requires adaptation not only just to keep up with but to lead global competition in the provision of telecommunications services and equipment. A new Teleglobe bolstered by Memotec will result in industry dynamism which will serve the interests of all Canadians and ensure that Canada remains a world leader in telecommunications.
It is important that Members recognize the urgency and importance of this legislation. The employees have also brought it to our attention that they want this legislation passed. I thank the House for assisting the Government and suggesting that the Bill be passed with expediency.

Mr. Speaker, in my opinion the question of the transfer of the pension to Memotec is serious. I have the letter alluded to this morning by the Member for Gander- Twillingate (Mr. Baker). It is indeed true that the employees are satisfied with the Memotec offer and the arrangements for their pensions.
My question concerns something that has bothered many of us. The actuarial assumptions which were made in 1980 and used for transferring the pensions from Canadian Arsenals are not the same assumptions that are being used this time. The question is whether it is a 5 per cent rate and salary increase assumption, whether we are looking at a 3.5 per cent CPI, at a 6.5 per cent interest rate and so on. Actuaries have a very complicated formula, including mortality rates and other factors.
In the committee, the unions stated that there would be a shortfall of some $7 million to $8 million in the transfer of the funds to the new company.

March 30, 1987
Teleglobe Canada
In the letter to the Minister of State for Privatization (Mrs. McDougall) on March 27, which was signed by Carlos Saldanha and E.A. Rutherford, it is stated:
-it is in the best interest of the parties concerned that Bill C-38 be passed and come into effect by March 31,1987.
That is true. The reason is the Quebec stock option plan, and it will be more easily saleable if they can roll this new asset and equity of Teleglobe into the Memotec assets.
We are not trying to prevent the passage of the Bill, but trying to understand exactly how the Government came to the logic of using new actuarial assumptions. How can one who is uninitiated in the matter-I am no actuary-justifiably say that, until the date of agreement, which is the proclamation of this Bill, prior service under the Public Service Superannuation Act is fully covered? The Minister of State for Privatization states that in the letter she sent to all employees on March 27. She states on page 3:
For those employees who choose to transfer their prior service credits to the Memotec "mirror" plan, the government will transfer the greater of twice the employee's contributions plus interest or the actuarial value of the accrued benefits computed on a going concern basis that recognizes future salaries and indexing and includes a provision for survivor benefits;
The next paragraph is key:
This amount will be fully adequate to allow Memotec to pay all of the obligations for prior service benefits;
Will the Hon. Member, who just spoke on behalf of the Government, request that the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. de Cotret) come to the House to confirm that indeed he fully gives to the employees the guarantee that he will sit down with them and explain what he means by a guaranteed prior service fully covered pension plan? Then there will be no difficulty in letting the Bill go through today. Will the Member give an undertaking that he will call his Minister, as I tried this morning, to have him come to the House this afternoon and give us an undertaking that prior commitments will be kept and the plan will be fully funded on the basis of actuarial assumptions?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there were many points in the Hon. Member's question, but I will attempt to answer him.
First, the Hon. Member alluded to the fact that there are a number of areas of input in developing an actuarial assumption. I, too, am not an actuary. Certainly, the Treasury Board must change and establish those assumptions from time to time, based upon all these inputs that are given, including interest rates and other factors.
I would not want to confuse anyone in that there are $7 million or $8 million involved. The Minister said it would be twice plus interest or actuarial assumption. Certainly, twice plus interest is much increased by the actuarial assumption. The example I referred to earlier was of the Treasury Board official who left the federal Government and went to work at a university. The best he would get would be twice plus interest. This transfer has a much greater transfer of past
service than that through the actuarial assumptions. We must make sure we put these things in the right place.
I want to re-emphasize that what is important here is that employees are attempting to get everything they possibly can. They are receiving total protection under the Labour Code. They are able to buy stock and receive the equivalent to the PSA Superannuation Program. They are looking for something that is different than has been set up by the actuarial assumptions established by Treasury Board. It is not like it is our money. That money belongs to the fund of all the other employees working for the Federal Government. Do we keep doing this even though it is not a right and proper actuarial assumption based upon sound calculations? If it is given to those few employees, there is going to be less in the fund for others.
Mention has been made of the Minister coming and speaking to the situation, and I am sure we shall carry on with the debate.

subtopic: TELEGLOBE CANADA REORGANIZATION AND DIVESTITURE ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, what we have with the decision to sell Teleglobe, which has been a Crown corporation, publicly owned, since its inception, is another example of the belief of the Conservative Government that the private sector can operate much more efficiently than the public sector and that wherever possible Crown corporations should be sold and privatized. That really ignores a great part of the history of the development of this country.
At the federal, provincial and municipal level we have several thousands of Crown corporations in Canada. They have been a way in which governments-and let me make it clear, not just socialists governments, but Liberal, Conservative, Social Credit, P.Q., CCF, and N.D.P. Governments- have set up Crown corporations when they saw a need to serve the public and when it was obvious that the private sector was not interested because it could not see that it could make a profit. After all, that is the reason private companies are established. I do not question that reason.
Therefore, what we have are Crown corporations which operate electric-power systems in our provinces. In the Province of Ontario, Ontario Hydro was set up, not be some radical socialist government but by the Conservative Government of the day. The three prairie provinces, Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta, have publicly-owned Telephone Systems. In my Province of Manitoba, the Manitoba telephone system was set as a publicly-owned utility by a Conservative Government in the year 1908. That was a government headed by Sir Roblin, the grandfather of Senator Roblin.
The Canadian National, a publicly-owned railway, was set up when a number of privately-owned and operated railway companies found they could not make a profit and were going bankrupt. The government of the day brought those companies
March 30, 1987

together and established the Canadian National as a publicly-owned system.
The Canadian Wheat Board was an agency set up by the Conservative Government headed by the Prime Minister at the time, the Right Hon. R. B. Mr. Bennett, to handle the sale of grain.
This was done because governments of the day, regardless of their political persuasion, realized there was a need because the private sector would not enter the field. These Crown corporations have provided a needed service and have helped develop this country in a way which would not have been possible had we depended entirely on the private sector.
I am sure there is no one in this House and no one in any political Party who has not realized that for the foreseeable future, for as many years as we can see in advance, we are going to operate in this country, as is the case in most countries, with a mixed economy in which there will be public ownership at the federal, provincial and municipal level-cooperative ownership-and in the main, privately-owned companies operating in most facets of Canadian life. We accept that. We do not say that because a certain Crown corporation was established recently or years ago for a very good reason it must always continue as a Crown corporation. We must ask ourselves if the Crown corporation provides a useful service and if it is operating efficiently.
We have to ask ourselves if the Government made its decision to sell Teleglobe after examining, as it should have done, what it was doing and whether it was operating efficiently? 1 do not think so. It seems to me that the Government was more concerned with achieving a quick sale of this Crown corporation, and others, than in linking any sale of Crown corporations to a well-thought out industrial policy, or after considering what the effect of the sale of Teleglobe would have on competition in the area of telecommunications.
Let us look at the record of the Government. It sold Cana-dair and de Havilland, companies in which governments, because they believed-and there was not much opposition to that belief-that in a modern industrialized country like Canada we must have an aerospace industry. When these two companies, which were earlier privately owned, decided that they could not make a profit and, therefore, they wanted to close down, the government of the day was, I think, almost unanimous in support of taking over these companies. Hundreds of millions of dollars were invested in research to make these companies efficient, in order for them to produce products which were state-of-the-art and could compete in the world market.
Fishery Products International was a publicly-owned corporation established because the private sector fishery companies were going bankrupt. Having bought these companies, and after the people of Canada paid hundreds of millions of dollars to keep these companies going, they were sold at a fraction of their cost.
Teleglobe Canada
The Government is now talking about privatizing the CNR and Air Canada. The objective when these two companies were taken over as publicly owned corporations was that they provide service to the people of Canada. That will go by the boards because as private companies they will be required to make a profit. One cannot object to this since shareholders of companies are entitled to gain a profit from their investment. However, service to the slow growth, have-not areas of the country will be drastically cut back. We have already seen that with regard to both the railways and the airline.
Let us take a look at the situation with regard to Teleglobe. Teleglobe is a Crown corporation responsible for all overseas telecommunications entering and leaving Canada. These include telephone, telegraph, cable and telex communications. Teleglobe is a joint owner of submarine ocean cables and telecommunications satellite systems. It has an effective monopoly in Canada on all overseas telecommunications. Overseas telephone calls account for 85 per cent of its revenues.
Was Teleglobe operated efficiently? Was it a money-loser or was it a money-maker? Teleglobe has always been a consistent money-maker. It has been known as the jewel of Crown corporations. In 1985 it recorded profits of over $53 million. Its profit picture for the last 10 years has been excellent. In 1985 Teleglobe's revenues totalled $678 million.
The Conservative Government has sold Teleglobe to Memotec Data, a small Montreal-based data processing and data communications company. The Government claims to have sold Teleglobe for $608 million. However, if we analyse the sale more carefully we will find that at most Memotec is paying $488 million for the company. Indeed, since Memotec as part of the purchase price has said it will assume Teleglobe's liabilities, which amount to $143 million, we must then estimate that the Government will only receive $345 million for Teleglobe. No actual funds will be paid for the debt.
We believe this is a low purchase price. The company's book value is reported to be anywhere between $300 million and $400 million. Furthermore, its sale value is much higher, as it has had, as I have indicated, an extremely profitable picture. We have been told that some time ago British Telecom made a bid of $750 million for the company.
Government and analysts thought that Teleglobe would bring in at least $600 million, and expected that it would receive that price. Unfortunately, the Government has let the company go for just one-half of that. The $600 million mark also explains why the Government has tried in its press coverage to create the impression that the company is being sold for more than $600 million.
We are completely opposed to the sale of Teleglobe because the company has been a consistent money-maker, because it is a monopoly and because it occupies the field of communications in which there is a legitimate public policy interest to be

March 30, 1987
Teleglobe Canada
protected. It adds insult to injury to receive only a paltry $350 million for such a lucrative company so valuable to the people of Canada.
There was a great deal of surprise about the sale of this company to Memotec. Memotec is just a minnow in the sea when compared with Teleglobe. In 1985 Memotec reported revenues of just $17 million. We must compare this figure to the $678 million in revenues reported by Teleglobe for the same year. We have to wonder how Memotec will manage this acquisition of Teleglobe. In Canada and in the United States we have seen companies which have gone in for these acquisitions and have done so by borrowing huge amounts of the money required from banks and other companies, and have then had tremendous difficulties in meeting the interest costs and showing a profit.
We have another problem with this sale. Teleglobe was the company which dealt with the international telecommunications business as a result of agreements made and treaties signed with other countries. With the exception of Japan and the United States, in countries which include Australia, New Zealand, France, West Germany, Italy, Norway and Sweden, there are government-controlled overseas telecommunications systems. In Great Britain the British Government has completed a major privatization of British Telecom through a share offering. However, the British Government retained just slightly more than 50 per cent ownership in the company. Thus it has a controlling interest.
Canada is a party to a treaty called the INTELSAT Treaty. INTELSAT is the international body which was set up in 1964 to govern all international overseas telecommunications satellite traffic. A key objective of INTELSAT is to provide even the most remote areas of the world with access to the global communications system. Therefore, services are to be provided at the same cost in high density traffic regions, for example industrialized countries, as in lower traffic regions. Essentially, the INTELSAT Treaty provides for a crosssubsidy system by which the richer countries subsidize the poorer ones.
With a U.S. satellite set up a privatized Teleglobe, which has as its goal the bottom line and profits for its shareholders, could well be in a conflict of interest situation. On the one hand it is supposed to represent Canada internationally on INTELSAT and carry out Canadian policy. On the other hand, it could be tempted to send at least some of its calls overseas via the cheaper U.S. systems. Its obligations to its shareholders would almost demand this, we believe, if going through the U.S. would be more lucrative. While Teleglobe could always endeavour to remove itself from INTELSAT, how would Canada then fulfil its international obligations? That question has not been dealt with.
I now wish to deal with the position of the employees. Memotec has agreed to provide current Teleglobe employees with a pension plan which is the equivalent to that which they currently have under the Public Service Superannuation Act, which is a good pension plan. Unfortunately, despite comments
made by the previous speaker, an Hon. Member from the Conservative Party, future employees of the company will not be eligible for this equivalent pension plan. For new employees there is to be a pension plan equivalent to the norm "in the telecommunications industry" in Canada. In other words, what we will see created after this deal is completed is two classes of employees, one with a respectable pension plan and the other with a less generous one. There are no job guarantees past the five-year period provided for in the Bill.
The employees are not very happy with the arrangements made with regard to their pensions. They point out that the arrangements made here are not the same as those made in other cases where the Government has divested itself of Crown corporations. Let me point out some examples.
In the case of Veterans Hospital, which was turned over to municipal operations, the employees were allowed to retain their Public Service pensions; in the sale of Canadian Arsenals, the purchaser and the union were able to negotiate a pension plan which allowed for the same kinds of benefits as a public service pension.
It should be recognized that most people had no concern about the growth or success of the purchasing company after privatization. With the Teleglobe sale, the Government is saying, as it did in the case of the sale of Canadian Arsenals, that they are protecting the employees. It is being said that they are offering the employees of Teleglobe everything offered to the employees of Canadian Arsenals, other than that in respect of the level of future additions.
The employees at Teleglobe have not negotiated with Memotec Data Incorporated, and they are feeling very insecure. There is no guarantee that Teleglobe will have the monopoly protection that the Government has suggested. Already Bell Canada and some provincial telephone companies are talking about bypassing Teleglobe; in other words, going through the United States.
So, there is no guarantee of success, and the employees feel that they are leaving a secure and growing pension plan for something smaller and less secure. Even if they could be guaranteed the protection which was theirs under the Pension Benefits Standards Act, they might accept.
The employees of Teleglobe have made their position clear: they are unhappy. They are unhappy about the lack of job security. There is no guarantee that Memotec will be able to grow and, even if it gets more business, that it will protect the job security of the present employees.
For all of these reasons, Mr. Speaker, it is our intention to oppose this Bill.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, let me say that we believe that Teleglobe has proven itself an effective money-maker, and as such we do not know why it should be sold. The long range outlook is that the company will stay a monopoly beyond the five year guarantee. There simply is not the demand in Canada
March 30, 1987

to have another overseas telecommunications service. Teleglobe is, effectively, a utility company, and therefore should remain in public hands, as do some of the telephone companies-

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I should like to address some comments on the remarks made by my friend from Winnipeg North. It may be that there will be a question come out of all of this.
I am a little concerned about the paper that he read from when he talked about the sale price being $350 million. It was $488 million, plus $100 million in returned profit, plus $18 million. Those are very right and proper figures. We have to be careful about the figures that some researcher gave to him. I am wondering whether his researcher read the proceedings of the legislative committee on this Bill. Certainly, the sale price was not an issue of any consequence during committee consideration of the Bill. There may have been one question on it. Certainly there was no lengthy discussion or questioning on the sale price itself. In fact, a Member of his own Party made the statement in committee that it was a very reasonable price.
Also, there was no argument mounted against the selling of Teleglobe by the employee group. Certainly, they had some thoughts and questions, but not about the sale itself.
It has been stated by the Minister, and it was stated in testimony by the President of Memotec, that there would be an equivalent pension plan put in place. The fact of there being an equivalent pension plan was not in issue. What was in issue was the actuarial assumption used in respect of past service. Certainly, it has been stated that there will be an equivalent pension plan for the employees. The only issue is whether the actuarial assumptions would result in sufficient moneys being transferred into the pension plan to handle all of the eventualities that actuaries attempt to calculate in setting up a pension plan.
Given that there was no argument mounted during committee consideration of this Bill in respect of the intelligence of selling Teleglobe Canada, given that the employees did not come before the committee to mount an argument against selling Teleglobe Canada, and given our experience with de Havilland and Fishery Products International, where privatization has resulted in added employment, why does the Party of which my friend from Winnipeg North is a member continue to talk against privatization?

subtopic: TELEGLOBE CANADA REORGANIZATION AND DIVESTITURE ACT
speechtext:
Let me try to deal with both points raised. With regard to the pension plan, let me put on the record a few paragraphs from the brief presented to the legislative committee which dealt with this Bill by the Communications and Electrical Workers of Canada, on March 10, 1987. Under the
Teleglobe Canada
section headed "Vested Rights and Collective Agreements", the brief reads:
-we were told that the purchaser had made a commitment to provide a pension plan identical to the Public Service Superannuation Plan-and the Supplementary Retirement Benefits Plan-for all current employees of Teleglobe Canada.
Our position is that all measures taken to make this affirmation a concrete reality should be defined and tabled to the unions representing those employees before the Bill is passed, in order to avoid any ambiguity.
I do not think that that was done. They go on to say:
We think plans identical to the PSSA and the SRBA should be offered to future employees as well (as current ones), to avoid treating them in a discriminatory manner.
That is exactly what I said in my remarks. The brief continues:
So far we have yet to see concrete written proposals from Memotec or the government with respect to the pension plan that will be introduced; that is why we think all such questions ought to be settled before the final passage of Bill C-38.
The CEWC considers that all rights and privileges currently enjoyed by Teleglobe's employees, and more especially those in Local 1653, must continue to apply, and that the government should make every effort required to ensure complete openness about this aspect of the matter.
Insofar as the point made about the price paid, let me read to the House the position which our researcher has given to us. It is as follows:
Memotec is to pay $488.3 million to the Government for the Teleglobe, and then the Government is to get $102 million in accumulated cash out of the company, plus an $18 million dividend, for a total of $608.3 million. But, these latter payments cannot be considered part of the purchase price, because they represent funds already in Government hands held by the crown corporation.
However, it is also understood that Memotec, as part of the $488.3 million purchase price, has said that it is assuming Teleglobe's debt liabilities, which amount to $143 million. If this is the case, then the government will only really be receiving $345 million for Teleglobe, as no actual funds will be paid for the debt. Memotec has said that it plans to raise the $345 million by a loan of $225 (million) from the National Bank, and an issue of $125 (million) in debentures to institutional investors.
That, Mr. Speaker, is precisely the point I made in saying that we can have real doubts as to whether Memotec can make this financial arrangement work.
