Mr. Speaker, last week Canada's First Ministers missed their opportunity for greatness. With few exceptions, insufficient political will and vision among our government leaders prevented the breakthrough which would have recognized in our Constitution the aboriginal right to self-government. The federal Government's mind-set was predicated on failure. Preparations for the conference were inadequate and the federal strategy became one of damage control.
The aboriginal peoples of Canada lost nothing at the conference. They emerged strong and united with all their rights intact. The Canadian Confederation lost, and our international reputation in the field of human rights has suffered.
We must try again, but this time with strong federal leadership and advocacy. The first step must be an agreement between the federal Government and aboriginal leaders. Once that is done, work can begin on a program of persuasion so that when another conference is called there will be unanimity that constitutional recognition of aboriginal self-government in this country is long overdue.

Mr. Speaker, last night 1,200 people jammed the Concert Hall of the Royal York Hotel in Toronto to watch two films dedicated to the 1.5 million Armenians killed at the hands of the Ottoman Empire in the first genocide of the 20th century.
The 60,000 Canadians of Armenian origin ask us to recognize and acknowledge their tragedy, not just for the sake of Armenians but for the sake of all mankind. There is a lesson here of what can happen when Governments and people are indifferent to the plight of religious and ethnic minorities.
In 1939, on the eve of his invasion of Poland, Adolf Hitler told his generals to show no mercy "because who, after all, speaks today of the annihilation of the Armenians?" The Armenians perished during World War I, the Jews during World War II.
March 30, 1987

Canada has recently spoken out eloquently about the Jewish Holocaust. Isn't it time for us to speak out just as eloquently about the Armenian Holocaust?

subtopic: HAIDA ARTIST'S REFUSAL TO PROCEED WITH NEW WASHINGTON EMBASSY COMMISSION
HAIDA ARTIST'S REFUSAL TO PROCEED WITH NEW WASHINGTON EMBASSY COMMISSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Bill Reid, a world-renowned Haida artist, has reminded us that art is not simply a commodity which can be bought and sold or produced on demand. Art springs out of the life of an individual or of a people. As an artist, Bill Reid believes that when Canada refuses to recognize the legitimate rights of the Haida people, Canada has no right to display Haida art in its embassies around the world. Because the First Ministers' Conference on Aboriginal Rights has failed, Mr. Reid has said that he will not proceed with a commission for a sculpture using Haida motifs and symbols which was to have been placed in the new Canadian embassy in Washington.
Mr. Reid has made this decision at great personal cost, both in terms of money and also in terms of international recognition of his work. But Bill Reid keeps two things more important than either money or fame. These are his integrity as an artist, and a living relationship with his people.
When will the Government of Canada come to terms with aboriginal nations so that the work of artists like Bill Reid can be shown in Canadian embassies and be seen as a symbol, not of colonial usurpation but of a living partnership among peoples?

Mr. Speaker, life is priceless. Since 1975, according to Statistics Canada, there have been an average of 60,000 abortions a year. It is crystal clear that abortion is the number one killer in Canada. The film, Eclipse of Reason, focuses on second-trimester abortion. I should point out that over 6,000 unborn Canadian children are aborted in the second or third trimester of pregnancy. This film shows quite graphically the manner in which they are killed.
Dr. Nathanson has stated, "Abortion, all abortion, is violence, and violence is impermissible in a world of reason. Late abortion, the systematic and deliberate destruction of a viable foetus, is especially odious". I agree with his statement
and applaud his efforts to show all of us the hard, cold truth about the procedure known as therapeutic abortion.
I urge all Members of the House to attend the film presentation today and see for themselves that abortion violently destroys a living human being. I am pleased to note that Dr. Nathanson is with us in the Gallery today.

Hon. Warren Allmand (Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine
East): Mr. Speaker, aboriginal nations left last week's First Ministers' Conference disappointed and frustrated. All aboriginal organizations, Indian, Inuit, Metis, and non-status, could not accept the final amendment proposal which was in part a complete contradiction of their long-standing position that they have an inherent right to self-government. They exercised this right prior to the arrival of the Europeans, never gave it up, and it was never extinguished.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) should have spent more time seeking a consensus acceptable to the aboriginal nations rather than one acceptable to opposing provinces. As a result he failed on both counts. Although this conference is over, Members of Parliament should continue to work with aboriginal groups in their pursuit of justice and fair play.

PARLIAMENTARY COMMITTEE'S REPORT-CRITICISM OF NEW DEMOCRATIC PARTY'S RECOMMENDATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, today the Special Committee on Child Care tabled its report along with its recommendations on government involvement in assisting Canadian families in the care of their children. Throughout our hearings Canadians told us they did not want the Government making decisions on how they would bring up their children, but they asked for assistance when it was needed.
No one attempted to advise us on how to differentiate between needs and wants, although in reviewing parts of the NDP wish list it would appear they are dealing with wants and not needs. Their definition of affordable is, "Cost should not be a barrier to access. Parental fees should diminish over a period of time until they are ultimately phased out." That means complete government involvement.
Neither do they subscribe to the fact that parents may be the best decision-makers concerning their own children. In fact in January they called for the resignation of the Minister of

March 30, 1987
National Elealth and Welfare (Mr. Epp) because he dared to make that suggestion. What hypocrisy! Canadians do not subscribe to that kind of thinking. Today's report goes some way toward addressing people's needs and is conscious of the Confederation of which we are so proud.

Mr. Speaker, over the weekend many of us heard the program on CBC which gave a description of the situation of homeless children. The example used was that of Winnipeg but the problem is not restricted to Winnipeg. It is a national problem. These kids are on the street. They prostitute themselves for meals and shelter. They use chemicals to escape harsh reality.
There is no reason why a country like this cannot take care of all its children. Canadians are relatively comfortable. The report was extremely disturbing and should prod us into action. We must have specific policies in order to make service available to these children while they are on the streets. We also must have policies designed to attack poverty so that children will have decent homes in which to live. I call upon the Government to take leadership in this area so that we have no more homeless children in our country.

Mr. Speaker, contrary to lead articles, and unlike Members of the Opposition and certain people who attended the recent Prime Ministers' Conference on native peoples, I for one consider that it proved to be a worthwhile and profitable exercise in several respects. First, it enabled the native groups themselves to take counsel together, for they must strengthen the ties that bind them so as to form a common front in the quest for the settlement of their claims. Then it made it possible for the provincial premiers to weigh their different views on the question of self-government of the first nations and set up a real mechanism to resume negotiations in the coming year. It also made it easier for Canadians to become better acquainted with the whole matter of native peoples' right to self-determination and understand that the Canadian conference cannot operate without Quebec.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, it made it possible for all Canadians to appreciate the leadership of our Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) who advocated a logical formula from which all
Parties can draw inspiration if they really want to find a solution to this basic question of the right of the first nations to self-determination.

subtopic: ACID RAIN-PRIME MINISTER'S SCHEDULED MEETING WITH UNITED STATES PRESIDENT
ACID RAIN-PRIME MINISTER'S SCHEDULED MEETING WITH UNITED STATES PRESIDENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in looking at the world of acid rain it is interesting to note that it took the United States a short time to negotiate a treaty to control acid rain which crosses its border from Mexico. This means that when the shoe is on the other foot the United States knows how to get fast action on acid rain.
This is an important fact to keep in mind on the eve of the third Summit. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) should, in his discussions with President Reagan, ask some pointed questions about the U.S.-Mexico deal to regain the ground he lost when he went out of his way two weeks ago in praising President Reagan for now keeping a promise made a year ago to spend money next year on research and demonstration.
By not restraining himself the Prime Minister gave away his negotiating position at the Summit. It is now time to regain the lost ground and openly and frankly demand acid rain cuts which will be meaningful to Canada.

maintopic: CANADIAN TEAM WINS WORLD WOMEN'S CURLING CHAMPIONSHIP
CANADIAN TEAM WINS WORLD WOMEN'S CURLING CHAMPIONSHIP
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Canadians enjoy, support, and indeed participate in the full range of local and international athletic competitions. Athletics make a substantial contribution to personal good health, to building the fabric of our country, and to presenting a favourable image of Canada abroad.
Such a happy event occurred this past Saturday which merits the applause of all Canadians. A team of young women representing the Racquet Club of Victoria, the Province of British Columbia and, most important, Canada, won the World Women's Curling Championship held in Chicago. The Pat Sanders rink of Victoria, which includes as a key member the niece of a distinguished Member of this House, overcame with courage, perseverance, and great skill all the challenges before it. Members of this House, indeed all Canadians, salute them.
March 30, 1987

maintopic: CANADIAN TEAM WINS WORLD WOMEN'S CURLING CHAMPIONSHIP
speechtext: Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, action against racism in our country is an urgent necessity. The multiculturalism sector sponsored a conference last July to consider strategy in race relations. Participants at the Winnipeg gathering urged strong action by the federal Government. There was debate between those who think that the primary challenge is to sensitize Canadians to these issues and those who believe minorities need to be empowered to grapple with systemic discrimination.
The Minister responsible for Multiculturalism (Mr. Crombie) has failed to resolve this debate. He has not yet stated what his race relations strategy is. Members of Canada's ethnocultural communities have been largely disappointed in the multicultural policies of the Government. Members of the visible minority communities have even less reason to be pleased. They have heard a lot of talk but have seen very little action.
I call on the Minister responsible for Multiculturalism to develop a strategy for overcoming racism in this country and to tell us what it is. The social situation becomes more urgent with every passing day.

Mr. Speaker, last week two very important environmental conferences were held in Quebec City. I refer to the National Wildlife Federation and the fifty-second North American Wildlife and Natural Resources conferences. Both organizations have their head offices in Washington, D.C.
Over 1,000 delegates were present and most were American. They heard the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and our Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan) speak forcefully on acid rain saying that the United States must do more to reduce its emissions, specifically that action should be taken by the White House and the U.S. Congress to enact legislation which will reduce U.S. emissions falling in Canada by 50 per cent by 1994. Estimates of these emissions are about 4 million tonnes annually.
Canada and four provinces, P.E.I., Newfoundland, Ontario, and Quebec, have already signed agreements to this effect to reduce their S02s by 1994. Manitoba is expected to sign very shortly. New Brunswick and Nova Scotia have not signed as
yet. However, our Minister of the Environment recently met with Premier Buchanan of Nova Scotia to discuss this. The Special Committee on Acid Rain has invited Premier Richard Hatfield of New Brunswick to appear before it on Thursday, April 2. This is another example of great progress being made on the serious problem of acid rain reduction.

subtopic: SOUTH AFRICA-ADVERTISEMENT PUBLISHED BY THE GLOBE AND MAIL
SOUTH AFRICA-ADVERTISEMENT PUBLISHED BY THE GLOBE AND MAIL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this morning, in a full-page ad in The Globe and Mail, the representative of the Government of South Africa said goodbye. He urged Canadians to go to South Africa to see that virtual nirvana will be found there for black people.
The Globe and Mail printed this ad at a cost to the South African Government of $29,000. Of course its defence will be freedom of the press, but I ask The Globe and Mail to seek fairness as well and accord gratis to the other voices from South Africa equal space to tell the truth.

Mr. Speaker, since the debate in the House on new trade arrangements a couple of weeks ago, I have sensed in my riding of Guelph and elsewhere in Canada a growing awareness of the importance of the Government's trade initiatives, both with the United States and the multilateral discussions under GATT.
The debate clarified many points. We learned that our agricultural marketing systems were not on the table. We learned once again that our social programs were not in jeopardy. We learned that protectionism in the United States was strong and growing stronger. We put to rest the Liberal and NDP concerns about the Auto Pact.
The debate strengthened the Government's resolve to protect Canadian sovereignty while promoting Canadian jobs. We learned that the NDP is afraid of American competition. We tried to learn where the Liberals stood. Following the debate, Canadians from all walks of life have come forward to say: "We can compete. Let us get on with it".
Oral Questions CULTURAL AFFAIRS

March 30, 1987

maintopic: DONATIONS TO MUSEUMS AND ART GALLERIES-POSSIBLE EFFECT OF TAX CHANGES
DONATIONS TO MUSEUMS AND ART GALLERIES-POSSIBLE EFFECT OF TAX CHANGES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the provisions of the Income Tax Act and the Cultural Property Export and Import Act encourage, through tax incentives, Canadians to donate works of art or other cultural property to public institutions in this country.
The fair market value as determined by the Cultural Property Export Review Board for the last year amounted to some $17.5 million in respect of some 430 donations.
It will be interesting to find out whether changes rescinding the exemption from capital gains tax on certified cultural property for taxpayers who are required to use the minimum tax calculation will adversely affect the generosity of Canadian donors.
In the meantime, let us thank those people who have done so much to enhance the stock of cultural property held by Canadian museums and art galleries.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Leader of the Opposition):
subsubtopic: CONSTRUCTION OF DAY CARE CENTRES ACROSS CANADA- GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the official document released by the Prime Minister during the last election campaign contained a promise-the words are those we read in the document-to find a speedy, realistic and effective solution to the pressing problem of child care.
This morning, almost three years later, the Conservative Members of this committee produced a report that fails to fulfil the promise made by the Prime Minister and fails to meet the pressing need for a national day care system.
Will the Prime Minister commit himself now, this afternoon, to building day care centres across Canada, because otherwise a national day care system is doomed to failure?

subsubtopic: CONSTRUCTION OF DAY CARE CENTRES ACROSS CANADA- GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, is the Leader of the Opposition serious about asking me to start building day care centres across Canada, when I received the report of a special committee of the House on child care, published under the title: "Sharing the responsibility", only a few minutes ago? Is he serious about having no hesitation about approving anything that can get the slightest bit of support for his party? Would he not prefer to take a more reasonable and sensible position? He could say, for instance, that now a report by a parliamentary committee has been submitted, we will take a quick look to see if the basic
criteria at the national level are met, and if that is the case, we will make some progress. If not, we will table a proposal in the House to give Canada a day care system that will help those who need it, first of all, and include conditions for providing for the necessary funding.
Interestingly ... I would like to hear what the Leader of the Opposition has to say about the taxes involved and the people who will have to pay for this extraordinary suggestion . . . Now he is being coached by the Hon. Member for Laval-des-Rapides. He certainly needs coaching because suggestions like that tend to raise expectations.

subsubtopic: CONSTRUCTION OF DAY CARE CENTRES ACROSS CANADA- GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: I can say to the Prime Minister that I am deadly serious because the recommendation of his members this morning did not respond in any way to the promises the Prime Minister made on behalf of his Party during the election campaign. Three years ago the Prime Minister's Government already had a report by Katie Cooke available and it has taken another three years to study the question once again.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext: Since Conservative Members this morning proposed virtually nothing to help moderate-income parents in their struggle to afford quality child care, will the Prime Minister question his members as to why in their report they gave no hope to the children of moderate-income families for quality day care services?
Hear, hear!
Mr. Speaker, I hear the "Hear, hears" from the other side. Reference was made to the Cooke Report. My understanding is that the implementation of that report would cost $ 11 billion a year.
That is right.

That is $11 billion a year, the equivalent of the total cost of the old age pensions. Is my right hon. friend saying he wants the Cooke report implemented today because he just referred to it so favourably? If he is, let him then stand up for the first time with some degree of responsibility and indicate to the Canadian people how he is going to pay for it.
Hear, hear!

What we have here is a bit of bravado to disguise the fact that the Conservative members of that committee have broken another promise of the Prime Minister. That is what we have. The Conservative members of the committee have ignored the need for national standards and a national plan for child care.
March 30, 1987

subtopic: REQUEST FOR FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL MEETING ON NATIONAL STANDARDS

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: REQUEST FOR FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL MEETING ON NATIONAL STANDARDS
speechtext: Will the Prime Minister meet urgently to obtain a federal-provincial consensus on national standards so that we can have a plan which responds on a national basis? Forget the bravado, forget the rhetoric, for once give us some action and response on one of the promises made by the Government.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL MEETING ON NATIONAL STANDARDS
speechtext:
The Right Hon. Leader says to forget the bravado, but he is also implying forget the facts, forget the costs. We are saying, no, you cannot have it both ways. You either have to be fiscally responsible and have low interest rates and growth or you are going to have the bankruptcy inflicted on the country by the Liberals in the past. You can't have it both ways.
You cannot have the hypocrisy of the Liberals on fundamental issues like this because some people, including the media, are going to begin asking you where you really stand. Do you want S11 billion a year expenditure here? If so, where are you going to get the money, because it will have to come from Canadians. It is time you started to tell them that.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL MEETING ON NATIONAL STANDARDS
speechtext: You made the promise.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL MEETING ON NATIONAL STANDARDS

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of National Health and Welfare. Is the Government prepared to table proposals that are more generous than those in the "Conservative" report tabled in the House this morning?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare

subtopic: REQUEST FOR CONSIDERATION OF LIBERAL MINORITY REPORT
REQUEST FOR CONSIDERATION OF LIBERAL MINORITY REPORT
speechtext:

speakeroldname: Hon. Jake Epp (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: REQUEST FOR CONSIDERATION OF LIBERAL MINORITY REPORT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in partisan politics there is always the temptation to give a quick response. As people have only had the report for a few hours I hope that they will study it in detail. By the same token I say to the Hon. Member, and, again, I do not know the entire proposal put forward by the Hon. Member and her Leader, if we are to trigger it only through the Canada Assistance Plan, even with the recommendations they make, then the problem becomes the following. Where is the turning point? What happens to families with gross incomes above that which have a number of children and in which both parents are working? Before people go shooting all over the place like rockets that find themselves with nowhere to go, I am simply saying that they had better be

March 30, 1987

careful that they analyse these matters carefully. Once that is done, the Government will come forward with a report.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister. More than 20 years ago we launched a universal medicare system in Canada which is the envy of most of the world. Today we should be doing precisely the same thing, based on the same principles, for child care. In the past we knew that we could not have medicare based on a system of tax breaks. My question to the Prime Minister is this. Since the Conservative majority on the committee which has just brought in its report advocates most of the government spending on child care come from a tax break system, will the Prime Minister now make it clear that he is committed to a universal, publicly effective system of child care, categorically reject this majority recommendation and say that the Government will put up money directly to provide the services our children need?
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, child care is a very significant and worthy national objective. We have discussed it. I have indicated that my Government is committed to it.
This report by parliamentarians came in only a few hours ago. In the tradition of parliamentary respect, we will want to read it and analyse it very carefully before responding.
As I have indicated in other circumstances-and I am delighted to do so again today-a child care program, which is something that cannot be instituted overnight, obviously, will require significant new resources. Notwithstanding that money has been rare in terms of its availability for new programs, we shall find, during the first mandate of this Government, the significant new resources necessary to ensure that, along with the provinces, we are on track in the development of a national child care program.
Hear, hear!
Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister knows that a fundamental question of principle is involved here.

Considering that 77 per cent of those who addressed the committee on the issue of funding opposed using the tax system to launch an important needed service such as child care, will the Prime Minister at least deal with that principle and say that we will do with child care what we have done with education in this country, what we have done with medicare in this country that is, not make it dependent on a specially calculated tax cut system but make it dependent upon direct government commitment?
Will the Government make that commitment now?
Read the report!

speakeroldname: Hon. Jake Epp (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Leader of the New Democratic Party dismisses the tax credit system, as he did in his question. I think it is important that it is understood by those following this debate that what he is saying is that he does not want a certain amount of the money that is to be put into child care to go directly to the parents, who will then decide, in their circumstances, what is best for their children.
It is easy to make those kinds of statements, but one has to analyse the effect. The first point that has to be made is that parents want to have some of those choices.
As the Prime Minister has said, it is obvious that we need more day care facilities; but I cannot accept the kind of response that the Leader of the NDP gives, with a cavalier rejection of the one side of the equation, that of parental choice. Those living in rural areas often have greater access to the extended family, and using the extended family for child care is a system that has worked well for them. Let us not deprecate that. Let's look at how we can extend that throughout our modern society, in giving to parents the choices that they need.

Since the Minister has chosen to answer, I can tell him that the arguments he has just given were arguments given by his Party against medicare when it was introduced more than 20 years ago. The same arguments were given in the 19th century against the introduction of a public system of education.
State ownership of children.
If the Minister reads our report, he will see that all kinds of options are given to parents. We want parental input into the decision on child care.
Hear, hear!

Since the Minister has chosen to answer, let me ask him if he will admit that 70 per cent of those who gave advice to the committee on this issue were turned down by the Progressive Conservative majority on the committee? And will he admit that 78 per cent of those appearing before the committee recommended against public funds going to profit-making day care centres and that that, too, was turned down by the committee?
Will he admit that he is not bringing in a universal system of child care but is, rather, going back to quaint old reactionary 19th century ideas, ideas almost innate to his Party.
State ownership of children.
I am prepared to have a battle on this one.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jake Epp (Minister of National Health and Welfare):

but he at least should have his history correct. If he goes back to the issue of hospitalization-

If one looks at page 342 of the Cooke report, it will be seen that the NDP propose to finance the $11 billion expenditure by, first of all, removing all dividends on any earnings of interest-and, by the way, the first $1,000 interest exemption is claimed by seniors; secondly, Mr. Speaker, they would propose that there be removed from RRSPs all tax benefits. For all Canadians RRSPs would be gone-
No, no.
Order.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Prime Minister.
The Prime Minister has said on at least three if not four occasions that "we shall have an effective child care system"; and he has also indicated-and I was very glad to hear this- that he will commit substantial resources to this end. He has said repeatedly: "an effective national child care system."
The major tax recommendations of this special committee do not reflect this promise of the Prime Minister's, nor do they reflect the views of most of the witnesses who appeared.
Oral Questions
I would like to ask the Prime Minister whether he will personally take the time to review these submissions; and further, will he ensure that the Government's response calls for federal funding for non-profit accessible quality child care as a top priority, rather than giving money away in tax breaks?
Hear, hear!
Mr. Speaker, indeed I will take the time to review this important report carefully, and I would hope that my hon. friend will do the same thing.
I already have. I wrote it.
The member opposite says that she wrote the report.
Not that one.

Well, maybe I will have to stand up and congratulate her, because she is breaking away from the NDP position of trying to nationalize our children. I can tell you, that we will not have. I want to congratulate the member for her enlightened position.
I cannot believe this! This is incredible.
I heard the Leader of the Liberal Party this morning talking about kidnapping children, and this is going one step further.
You didn't hear clearly.

The Prime Minister is aware of the various studies that have been done on day care, and many are repeated in the report he has in front of him. These studies show that non-profit child care is qualitatively better than "for profit" child care. Studies right across the country have shown this.
An. Hon. Member: Right on!

My question for the Prime Minister is: will he be sure, when developing this national child care program that he talks about, to ensure that this principle is embodied in the Government's national child care program?

Mr. Speaker, I indicated to my hon. friend, who has had a great interest in this subject over many years, the extent of the Government's commitment. For example, at the First Ministers' Conference held in Vancouver last year, I, on behalf of the Government, as I did on prior occasions, committed the Government of Canada to searching for ways, with the provinces, whereby, together, we could bring about a genuine and effective national child care system.

March 30, 1987
Oral Questions
I think all of the provinces, be they of NDP, Liberal, or Conservative background, acknowledged that the complexity and the financial burden implied in such a program were such that it could not be done overnight, but they viewed the approach of the federal Government or the commitment of the federal Government as one of very considerable importance, because it marked the beginning of that kind of program which would benefit Canadian families and Canadian parents so greatly. I tell my hon. friend that we will examine very carefully, not only this report, but the minority report submitted by my hon. friend, against the backdrop of the following commitment-that our commitment to a child care program is real and that Canada will find the resources to have an effective national child care program.

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR REOPENING OF DISCUSSIONS WITH ABORIGINAL LEADERS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Right Hon. Prime Minister. As the Prime Minister knows, last week's constitutional conference on aboriginal rights was doomed to failure almost from the outset. The key factor in that failure was his Government's unwillingness to accept the fact that aboriginal self-determination is an inherent and inalienable right. That is a vital and first step. There had to be at least a united front between the federal Government and the aboriginal leaders. Is the Prime Minister prepared to say today to the House and to the country that he will reopen discussions and negotiations with the aboriginal leaders without delay, so that a suitable and appropriate selfgovernment amendment could be found? Would he try, please, to get it right this time?

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR REOPENING OF DISCUSSIONS WITH ABORIGINAL LEADERS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we put forward the proposal on behalf of the Government of Canada that the constitutional amendment should reflect the existence of an explicit right. This position was endorsed by Governments of Liberal, NDP, and Conservative persuasion. It was viewed by the provincial Governments to which I just referred as the appropriate way to go. If my hon. friend is saying that I, as Prime Minister of Canada, should have accepted a constitutional amendment that provided for an undefined and immediately enforceable right to self-government giving rise to nation to nation sovereignty in Canada, that is an entirely different proposal. If he is putting forward that proposal, may I ask him if this is the position of the Liberal Party of Canada, the Official Opposition?
Mr. Speaker, the Right Hon. Prime Minister knows the position of the Liberal Party of Canada. It is in the motion-
Nobody else does.

The position of the Liberal Party of Canada and its Leader is clearly stated in the motion proposed by the Leader of the Opposition in the House just over a week ago; that is the position. Will the Right Hon. Prime Minister study that motion and will he accept it as being the route to follow, and engage in a program of persuasion to convince the Premiers of the country and the public that this is the kind of self-government amendment we want and need in order to complete this Confederation of ours?

Mr. Speaker, I am interested by the suggestion of my hon. friend. While I was not in the House at the time, I read Hansard. I think there was a question from the Minister of Justice addressed to the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition asking him if the position he had adopted meant that he espoused a position consistent with that put out by the AFN which has implications of sovereignty, nation to nation sovereignty. The Leader of the Opposition, as I understand it, rejected that proposal and rejected that position.
What we have put forward, endorsed by the Government of Ontario, by Premier Peterson, by his very distinguished Attorney General, by Premier Ghiz, and by the Leader of the Government in Yukon, the NDP, was a commitment which was far in advance of anything put forward before on behalf of the federal Government. If we compare it with the position in 1983 and 1984, we see a tremendous step forward on behalf of native rights coming from the Government of Canada.
I think that I share the view of Ontario Attorney General Ian Scott who said that history will show that Canada missed an excellent opportunity to entrench self-government, because the proposal we put forward, while not perfect, on behalf of the people of Canada and the Government of Canada, strongly endorsed by Ontario, Prince Edward Island, and others, would have marked in its acceptance a great stride forward toward equality and fairness for the native peoples of Canada. I deeply regret that we did not succeed, but I give my hon. friend the assurance that we shall try again to make sure that justice comes about for the native peoples of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of the Environment. As the Minister is aware, yesterday, shortly after midnight, a mysterious cloud
March 30, 1987

of toxic gas arrived in the southeast area of Calgary causing concern and illness to many of my constituents. speechtext: Yes, Mr. Speaker, I can give the Hon. Member the assurance he seeks. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are still looking for a formula that will make it possible to enshrine the rights of aboriginal peoples in the Constitution of Canada. We worked non-stop on a formula that would receive the approval of seven provinces with 50 per cent of the population. We did not succeed last week, but the federal Government's obligation is clear. I think the responsibility is equally shared by the provinces, and we intend to examine with them and the leaders of the various aboriginal groups the various alternatives available, in order to try and develop another formula that would meet with the requisite consent of the various groups so that this right can finally be enshrined in the Canadian Constitution.

March 30, 1987
Oral Questions

Mr. Speaker, by way of a supplementary question, the Prime Minister stated at the conference that the people who would bear the heaviest price for that failure were the native people of Canada. I would like to hear, and I am sure so would all Canadians, what the federal Government will do to ease that burden of failure that has been laid upon the native people of this country.

Mr. Speaker, I indicated that I thought the native peoples would bear the heaviest price, not because of their responsibility but because of our collective failure to achieve an agreement that would relieve them of that burden. I said with the greatest sadness that this was a moral obligation that has been unfulfilled by Canada, by the federal Government, by the provinces and so on.
I point out to my hon. friend that when the amending formula was devised, it was devised, of course, with the concept of 10 provinces involved. I want to tell my hon. friend how difficult it is when a province, which reduces the number to nine, with about 30 per cent of the population, is not part of the amending formula, of the process, and how few doors on which a Prime Minister can knock on behalf of the aboriginal peoples in trying to build that consensus which is necessary.
It may be that if we get the leadership and generosity from other provinces that we will be able, for example, to find a formula which will allow Quebec to become part of the constitutional process. In which case it is my judgment that that would greatly facilitate an equal degree of justice so long overdue to the native peoples, because the Government of Quebec is quite favourably disposed to many of the things that we have been trying to do over the last number of years.

subtopic: TELEGLOBE CANADA REORGANIZATION AND DIVESTITURE ACT

speechtext: The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mrs. McDougall (St. Paul's) that Bill C-38, an Act respecting the reorganization and divestiture of Teleglobe Canada, be read the third time and do pass.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
subtopic: TELEGLOBE CANADA REORGANIZATION AND DIVESTITURE ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will give my colleagues a choice: they can either listen to me or leave, but I hope at least 20 members will stay in the House!
Teleglobe Canada

We are dealing today with Bill C-38 which will give legislative authority for the sale of Teleglobe Canada to Memotec. This is a $600 million transaction. My preoccupation with this sale has mostly been with the question of pensions and the right of employees of the new company to a mirror plan pension equivalent to what they had when they were covered under the Public Service Superannuation Act.
The Bill is fundamentally flawed because it does not ensure in law that the employee compensation package will be fair, equitable and respectful with regard to the acquired pension benefits. The Government is attempting to rush Bill C-38 through the House and committee arguing that tomorrow, March 31, is a deadline for the deal, although the Bill has a June, 1987, date for finalization. The reasons are basically financial with regard to the Quebec stock option plan and the new rules which will apply on April 1 for those who invest in plans approved by the province. By blending the equity of Teleglobe, Memotec would change category and there may be some people who would have less interest in buying this stock under the Quebec stock option plan.
Nevertheless, the employee organizations to which I had the pleasure of speaking this morning have assured me that they have received a better deal from Memotec than they were originally offered by the Government. Although the Hon. Member for Sarnia-Lambton (Mr. James) said that they had not mounted a sustained attack on the Bill, their interest is to protect acquired rights in regard to pension and to protect their plan from being eroded by a pick and choose option of the Government with regard to actuarial assumptions and, more specifically, the interest rate and mortality rates.
This is a rather complex issue and for the average Canadian who has not been briefed it could be somewhat difficult to understand. I will try-

in French we say "vulgariser", and in English I would say [English]
-make it as simple as possible. I will use the KISS principle, "Keep It Simple, Stupid". The idea starts with actuarial assumptions.

And what are those actuarial assumptions? In the case of Memotec, we are talking about $100 million, a fairly substantial amount, that would be set aside for employees.
The Government, however, has decided against transferring the entire amount to the new company which would otherwise have had a fully funded plan. The Government is proposing to transfer only 90 per cent, on the basis of actuarial tables produced by the Chief Actuary of Canada in 1971. The Government has considered factors which we find hard to

March 30, 1987
Teleglobe Canada
reconcile with what we know today about the latest assessments made by Canadian actuaries of the Canadian Institute of Actuaries.
Regarding the first item, interest, the Government maintains that the interest rate proposed by the actuaries is too high and therefore wants to bring the rate down. Furthermore, the Government again, while recognizing that the GAM, which is a GAM 83, the-

-the Group Annuity Mortality.

So, what the Government did was to use GAM 71 instead of the far more recent GAM 83. The difference between GAM 71 and GAM 83 is that the latter study recognizes that the life expectancy of workers is far greater than it was in 1971. People are living longer and so will be entitled to pension payments for a longer period of time, and we must therefore provide for additional funding.
The latest GAM was a study prepared by the Canadian Institute of Actuaries in 1983, which recognizes, as I said before, that life expectancy has improved and people are living longer. The Government did not consider GAM 83 but GAM 71 because it was more convenient. According to GAM 71, people were dying at an earlier age which meant that the Government's outlay for pensions was not as high.
Mr. Speaker, perhaps I should explain that these actuarial assumptions are based on the following components. One component refers to interest, set at 6.5 per cent over the long term. Another component refers to long-term inflation of 5.5 per cent, and there is also a component that refers to wage and merit increases, in other words, advancement during a person's career, which is set at 1.5 per cent. Usually, inflation and wage and merit increases are about 5 per cent. This is important. It is this 5 per cent margin that is most often used by actuaries.
As I was saying earlier-and I am getting back to my point on interest rates-the Government feels that interest rates are too high and that nothing justifies investing as much as $100 million at current rates, which as we know are about 8 or 8.5 per cent, to produce that much money. Expecting the fund to yield more, the Government holds back the money, the Government helps itself and says: We will put back only 90 per cent because we believe that 6.5 per cent over a long term would be enough to meet pension commitments.
Well, Mr. Speaker, the union, the employees and management maintain that there is something wrong, something unfair in this Government approach. And this was, if you will, the basic argument of the union and the employers during the committee proceedings. They quite rightly maintained that indeed the employees had every reason to be concerned because, on one hand the company was committed to continue and maintain a plan identical to the one the employees had with Teleglobe, and on the other the company promised to maintain and give the same sound bases, the same financing
and the same benefits the employees had been enjoying all along.
What worries the unions and Memotec management is that if the $100 million actuarial fund were paid to the company there would probably be enough money to keep the fund on a sound actuarial basis. But if the amount paid is reduced to 90 per cent, $90 million instead of $100 million, the employee is quite justified to ask the following question: Will my savings, my money, my contributions be sufficient to guarantee the pension benefits I am entitled to in future years?
And this is an honest question, it is even very serious because ever since the committee sat we had to put up many arguments to convince the Government to listen. Mr. Speaker, in a 1986 telex to Teleglobe Canada employees concerning privatization, the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. de Cotret) had this to say: "Regarding your March 21, 1986 telegram, I assure you that I will be available to meet with you and answer the question on pensions before an announcement is made. As soon as my agenda is definite I will see to it that my office get in touch with you to set the time and place of the meeting." It is signed Robert de Cotret, President of the Treasury Board.
Mr. Speaker, the President of the Treasury Board had promised he would meet with the employees to re-assure them and explain the Government position concerning this transfer of pension funds, but he did not keep his word, he did not take this opportunity he had to give the employees more explanations. He sent his officials to do that, Mr. Speaker, and God knows the employees did their best, but these officials did not have authority to change anything and, since their hands were tied, they had to admit that only the Minister could solve the problem, that is come up with the $ 10-odd million to put the fund on a sound actuarial basis and do justice to Teleglobe-Memotec employees.
Mr. Speaker, not only the employees said that, so did management people, senior officials who belonged to the ad hoc committee. Here is a quotation from page 243 of the March 11, 1987 legislative committee proceedings on Bill C-
38:

I am a manager at Teleglobe. I am a member of the Ad Hoc Committee on Pension Matters. It was put together after 90 per cent of Teleglobe employees expressed their concerns about the way pension matters were evolving. The committee was formed to protect the pension benefits which had accrued and would continue to accrue.
The committee is representative of all employees, unionized and nonunionized, and those almost between two chairs. Possibly it is going to become a technical personnel association in the future.
It goes on in the next paragraph:
Why are employees concerned? 1 think we should talk about a few terms: pensions and acquired pension benefits.
Later in the same hearing on March 11, 1987, Mr. Rutherford said:
March 30, 1987

One more point. We also have been informed by government personnel that the actuarial methods used will be different from those used for Canadian Arsenals and that the results obtained by Teleglobe employees will certainly not be as favourable. They have tried to assure us that it will be close, but whether it will be close or not we have another actuary who says that maybe it will not be. We do not really know and understand why we would not get the same sort of treatment as Canadian Arsenals. It is discriminatory.
Indeed, it is discriminatory that the Government would have deux poids, deux mesures, or two weights, two measures. One set of assumptions was used for Canadian Arsenals and there was a good and fair settlement. A different set of figures was used for Teleglobe, another company being privatized by the Government. No wonder employees, managers and nonunionized people would join together to say that it is discriminatory. There must be one standard that will apply to all, otherwise it opens discussions and the possibility of this kind of discrimination.
After the committee stage, the Bill returned to the House at report stage where we moved an amendment that was defeated by the Government.
Today we began third reading. The Member for Sarnia- Lambton (Mr. James) said that in his opinion the unions had not mounted an attack against the privatization of Teleglobe. I think that statement will not bear scrutiny when one reads the reports of the various intervenors in the debate.
The Government has made a decision on privatization. It decided to sell Teleglobe and make S600 million to reduce the deficit. One of the union representatives stated in committee that this was like selling the furniture to pay the rent. Nevertheless, apart from the privatization debate, which I will not enter because my time is limited, I suggest it would have been a good occasion for the Government to show some sensitivity by meeting with the union representatives and others to better explain the transaction as it relates to their pension acquired rights.
Today we saw a letter from the Minister of State for Privatization, who is also Minister responsible for regulatory affairs, which was addressed to all employees of Teleglobe. We also saw the answer from Mr. Carlos Saldanha and Mr. Rutherford, whom I quoted before, on behalf of the Teleglobe Canada AD HOC Committee on Pensions.
I want to quote from those documents in order to clarify the situation. The Minister's letter to the employees, attempts to make the case that all employees will be protected fully by this transaction in regard to the continuity of their pension benefits. The Minister states in her letter:
Teleglobe employees will have the equivalent of a PSSA pension plan and more.
The Conditions of Sale required prospective purchasers to put in place a pension plan that was at least as good as the telecommunications industry norm;
Memotec is replacing the PSSA with a plan that mirrors these benefits for all existing employees;
1 accept that. The employees and some of us in the House are concerned that if less money than required is transferred to Memotec, perhaps some of the hard-earned savings will not be
Teleglobe Canada
there in five years when the monopoly in telecommunications will more or less have run out for that company. Our difference of opinion lies in the fact that the Government, in using the actuarial assumptions it has, literally reduces the actuarial transfers that will be given to the new company by some $10 million. That worries the employees today because it is possible the company could face some difficulties and fall short of the expectations that the Minister seems to imply. She goes on to say in her letter:
This means there will be no change to the current level of pension benefits enjoyed by Teleglobe employees. It is false and misleading to suggest that they are being deprived of benefits;
No one ever said that. We are saying that there is a shortfall and a use of figures which I do not believe is easily explainable in regard to the actuarial assumptions that have been changed, and with regard to the interest rate and the actuarial mortality rates. We know that Canadians are living longer. We must not try to make people believe that despite the fact that the actuarial studies show an increase in life expectancy, we will use some 1971 study to justify the transfer of funds. That is a measure of some concern.
I would like to make with a few closing remarks. I said that this Bill is discriminatory. I think the employees feel that in this transaction the effects of the actuarial assumptions will have a difficult and possibly damaging effect on their pension benefits. The President of the Treasury Board (Mr. de Cotret) could have solved that if he had kept his word and met with the employees and explained what he intends to do. That complaint not only comes from the unions, it comes from nonunion individuals and management. They all feel very nervous and concerned about this plan and would like the Minister to sit down with them-that is all they are asking-and explain and then come to an agreement and, if need be, have a third-party arbitrator to do that for the sake of protecting the integrity of the employees and their savings and pension benefits.

speechtext:

subtopic: TELEGLOBE CANADA REORGANIZATION AND DIVESTITURE ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have an opportunity to participate in the debate today on third reading of Bill C-38, an Act to authorize the sale of Teleglobe. I am pleased to have an opportunity to say a word about privatization, about the Government's privatization program in general and, more specifically, about the privatization of Teleglobe. I regret that the Minister of State for Privatization (Mrs. McDougall) did not take the opportunity, which was hers at third reading, to speak to the House, giving us the benefit of her reflections on this process and on
Teleglobe Canada
the proposal by the Government. In abdicating her responsibility to do so she gave the Hon. Member for Gander-Twillin-gate (Mr. Baker) the opportunity for unlimited time in which to make his remarks. Knowing the oratorical talent of the Hon. Member, I am surprised that that time did indeed come to an end and that he is not still speaking. One thing I would have liked to have heard from the Minister, if she had deigned to enter the Chamber and share her thoughts with ordinary Members of Parliament, would have been the Government's philosophy and over-all strategy with respect to the money that the Government will receive as a result of privatization sales.
In the fall of 1985 I had the opportunity to go with a parliamentary study group to Great Britain. I was there with the former Member for St. John's East, His Excellency the Lieutenant Governor of Newfoundland, and several others. I suppose I can refer to the former Hon. Member by name now since he is no longer a sitting member. Mr. McGrath was chairman of the delegation. We spent some time in London meeting with officials and politicians from both sides of the House to discuss the politics and the mechanics of privatization. We all know that the British Government committed itself to a privatization program which, in large measure, it has completed. A great many British Crown corporations have been privatized to one degree or another. I would note, however, that even the British Government and Mrs. Thatcher, whom we in my Party regard as being ideologically extreme with respect to economic matters, retained a 51 per cent controlling interest in British Telecom when they privatized it. Even Mrs. Thatcher was wise enough and pragmatic enough, one might say, to realize that when it comes to something such as communications, and in particular international telecommunications, the public interest must come before any particular ideological consideration or any particular opportunity for increasing the profit that might come to the Government through privatization. Thus the British Government retained a 51 per cent ownership in British Telecom. If I remember correctly, it privatized the other 49 per cent in the market-place through the offering of shares for sale.
When I was in Britain at that time there was a debate going on within the Conservative Party with respect to what should be done with the moneys received from privatization. It was a very interesting debate. One of the things I have found odd about the politics of privatization in Canada is that there has been no debate in Canada similar to that which went on in Britain. The privatization debate here in Canada seems to be somewhat of a sideline. It is something that is going on while other more important things are going on.
I find this regrettable for two reasons. The first is, of course, that I am opposed to the Government's privatization program. Quite frankly, I think it is getting away with murder. I think it is getting away with having all these privatizations, not having all that much attention paid to the process either by the media or by Parliament for that matter. I think these Bills have made their way through the parliamentary process with much less

March 30, 1987
Tele globe Canada
hassle than the Government deserves on its measures to privatize Crown corporations.
Having said that, what I found most interesting about the debate going on in Britain was the debate going on within the Conservative Party itself about where the money from privatization should go. As I understand the position of the Conservative Party of Canada-and if I misunderstand the position I hope government Members will correct me-it is that this money will simply go into operating revenues, into current accounts. This money will not be set aside for any specific purpose that might either now or later be determined by the Government to be a worthy object of such funds. Within the Conservative Party in Britain there was a debate about whether the money from privatization-and we are talking about considerable sums of money- should go simply into offsetting the deficit or whether it should go into a special fund created by these numerous privatizations. On the part of those Conservatives who were in favour of the special fund option, if I may put it that way, their thought was that they might be better able to persuade the public of the value of privatization if they could point to specific things that they were going to do with the money received from such sales.
The criticism of simply taking any money made from privatization and applying it to the deficit was best put by the late Lord Stockton, or Harold Macmillan, a former Prime Minister of Great Britain. During debate in the House of Lords, Lord Stockton compared the policy of the Conservative Government of Mrs. Thatcher to selling off the family silver in order to pay the electricity bill.
Yet, Mr. Speaker, this is exactly the kind of policy that we see coming from the Progressive Conservative Government here in Canada, the difference being that at least-and this is no ringing defence of the Conservative Party of Great Britain-at least within that Conservative Party, they were intellectually alive enough, or at least the 92 year olds were, to ask whether it was a viable strategy to take this money that was being made from the sale of important institutions and using it in this non-specific, non-goal oriented way of applying it against the current deficit. There was a great debate, and I was impressed with the way a 92-year old parliamentarian delivered a criticism of his own Government. I am probably not being faithful to the exact words, but certainly the analogy of selling off the family silver in order to pay the electricity bill was used.

And here, Mr. Speaker, we have a good example of how the Canadian Government is leaving itself open to this particular kind of criticism, leaving aside the more fundamental criticism of the Government's privatization program in the first place, a program with which we, as New Democrats, disagree. We disagree with it both in principle and in practice: in principle because we do not think that a
comprehensive privatization program is what is going to bring about the rebirth and necessary restructuring and revitalization of the Canadian economy; and opposition in practice because thus far none of the privatization that this Government has embarked upon has met what we would consider to be the condition under which isolated privatization might be to the benefit of Canada.
I say that, Mr. Speaker, because 1 want you and other Members to know-and I have said so in the House before- that we are not opposed, on principle, to each and every privatization that each and every Government might consider in each and every moment of Canadian history.
The Manitoba Government, for instance, only recently decided to privatize the Flyer Bus Company. It was felt that that was the only reasonable course of action left to the Government in the circumstances of that case.
It would be a mistake to imagine that this Government's privatization program is simply a matter of pragmatic judgment being made on a case-by-case basis, and what we do disagree with in principle is that privatization should be one of the main elements, or indeed an element, of the Government's over-all approach. We do have a fundamental difference with the Government in that respect.
The privatization of Teleglobe has proceeded without the kind of attention that a major privatization such as this should have received. Teleglobe is a Crown corporation which has been a consistent money-maker. Its sale raises the question of how Crown corporations cannot win when it comes to the Progressive Conservative logic in respect of Crown corporations. According to that logic, if a Crown corporation is losing money, it should be privatized, because obviously the Government cannot do a good job; and if a Crown corporation is making money, then it, too, is to be sold.
The only Crown corporations that fit into this strange Conservative cosmology when it comes to Crown corporations are those which exist in the twilight zone between profitability and bankruptcy.

I mentioned earlier, Mr. Speaker, the matter of this being an example, to use Lord Stockton's words, of selling off the family silver. Teleglobe has been regarded by many as the jewel of the Crown corporations. In 1985, it recorded profits of $53.2 million. Its profit picture over the last 10 years is a good one. In 1985, its revenues totalled $678 million.
One of the aspects that has not been considered often enough with respect to the sale of Teleglobe to Memotec, Mr. Speaker, is the international dimension of the services for
March 30, 1987

which Memotec will be responsible as a result of its ownership of Teleglobe.
I ask you, Mr. Speaker, to consider that Canada is a party to the INTELSAT Treaty. INTELSAT is the international body set up in 1964 to govern all international telecommunications satellite traffic. The key objective of INTELSAT is to provide even the most remote areas of the world with access to the global communications system. Its services are to be provided at the same cost in high density traffic regions as in lower density traffic regions. Essentially, the INTELSAT Treaty provides for a cross-subsidy system, with the richer countries subsidizing the poorer ones.
Another central purpose of the INTELSAT Treaty is to ensure that all member countries will direct their satellite traffic exclusively through INTELSAT.
Teleglobe has always been Canada's designated signatory to the INTELSAT operating agreement, and represents Canada on the INTELSAT Board of Governors. A privatized Teleglobe is to continue this role.
Recent developments in the United States, springing from the introduction of so-called competition in telecommunications in the U.S., have led to the U.S. deciding to renege on its commitment to INTELSAT. It will be putting up competing satellite systems, and these competing systems will not have cross subsidies in their rate structures.
With U.S. satellites set up, a privatized Teleglobe which has as its goal the bottom line profit for its shareholders could well be in a conflict of interest situation. On the one hand, it is to represent Canada internationally on INTELSAT, and carry out Canadian policy; on the other hand, it could be tempted to send at least some of its calls overseas via the cheaper U.S. system.
Its obligations to its shareholders would almost demand this, if going through the U.S. would be more lucrative. While Teleglobe could always endeavour to remove itself from INTELSAT, how would Canada then fulfil its international obligations?
Teleglobe has proved itself to be an effective money-maker. Why should we sell off the family silver for a very, very shortterm consideration on the part of this Government, for obviously purely ideological reasons, so ideological that they look extreme even in comparison to what has been done in Great Britain?
The privatization program of the Government should receive more attention than it has been receiving. I hope, this afternoon and in subsequent debate, that Canadians will awaken to the fact that what is happening under the Government is a basic restructuring of the economy. I do not think that this is always apparent.
Before my time is up, let me say that the days of the Conservative Government are numbered. But even if the

Tories are defeated at the next election, and if they are able to proceed with the economic agenda which they have before them now, through privatization, deregulation, and free trade, it worries me that they will have fundamentally reoriented Canadian economic thinking and restructured the Canadian economy.

March 30, 1987

and perhaps on that basis there has not been the kind of critical attention there should have been to the failure of the Government to have a coherent economic policy. At the same time, there has not been the kind of emphasis in the media that there should be that the Government is proceeding with its own very right-wing agenda of deregulating and privatization. The privatization of Teleglobe is a prime example. This Bill is a very clear example of privatization for no other reason than ideology. Teleglobe, as everyone in this House knows, has been a consistent money-maker. In 1985 it had earnings of $53.2 million. Teleglobe has been bringing money into the federal Treasury at a time when we are all concerned about the deficit. The company is a money-maker, and yet the Government is getting rid of it. It is killing the goose that laid the golden egg because the Government wants, I guess, to have a few quick dollars that will look good in reducing the deficit. In addition, Teleglobe performs a vital function in Canada's whole communications industry. Teleglobe is a vital link in international communications.
There are some very serious questions as to whether or not it is in the interests of the Canadian public that a vital link should go into private hands. The Government says it will regulate the company. On the one hand, the Government says we should be getting out of the whole area of deregulation and that we should be deregulating. On the other hand, it says it will privatize Teleglobe but will regulate it. There is a certain inconsistency here. I believe it would be much better if Teleglobe remained a Crown corporation earning money for Canadians, serving the general public interest in the whole field of telecommunications.
I do not wish to speak at any great length this afternoon, but I do want to emphasize the whole question of pensions. When I spoke at second reading on February 16, 1987, I noted the importance of the pension issue because I spoke to the employees of the earth satellite station in my constituency a year and a half ago. Teleglobe is being sold to Memotec. As our critic, the Hon. Member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell), pointed out, it is like a minnow swallowing a whale. Memotec is not a large corporation. It does not have a distinguished track record. There is a lot of concern about the future of Teleglobe in new hands. Does Memotec have enough clout to be able to maintain the monopoly position that Teleglobe has had? There are no guarantees in the Bill that that will happen. Naturally, employees are very worried about their protected pension plan now being transferred to Memotec, even though some of the provisions are good. I want to register my concern that the Government is proceeding with an ideological program for privatization when there are no rational reasons for the privatization of Teleglobe.
Teleglobe Canada
The Government is selling Teleglobe, this very important link in our communications industry, at a time when we see that it has made money for Canadians. We have to ask why. We do not see the reason. Mr. Speaker, I have a few words I would like to say on this legislation. Because of the Government's majority there is no doubt this Bill will go through. However, the Government has not done what any good employer would do to make sure its employees are well treated. It is allowing this sale to take place in such a way that it will be branded as a Government that allowed employees of 25 or 35 years to be sold off with the company and without the same kind of pension plan they had before.
I have heard the protestations of government Members, but we are still faced with the fact that there are employees of Teleglobe who are not satisfied that they have been treated properly. They have put more into the pension plan than they are going to be able to take out. Those employees will receive $7 million less than they would have received had the Government made the same arrangement in this sale as it did in the sale of Canadian Arsenals.
Teleglobe was established in 1949. Since that time, with the infusion of public funds, it has grown. Yet with this legislation we are going to allow a private corporation to reap the benefit of that infusion of public money. That is quite unacceptable to most people. The taxpayer has the right to expect to get most of that money back. That has not been allowed to happen in this particular case, and a very profitable company will be sold to another operation which has very little experience in operating this type of company.
There is something else of concern to us. Here we have a monopoly operation and I am a little surprised that the free enterprise philosophy of the Government did not hold in this case. Ordinarily, if that philosophy did hold, the Government would have sold the company to Memotec and left it to the rough and tumble competition of the communications marketplace. Instead, this company will remain under the control of the CRTC, but with only a partial guarantee of a monopoly. That bothers the employees of Teleglobe as well. There will be quite an opportunity for other companies to bypass Teleglobe when it becomes a private organization.
The Government suggests that it will guarantee a monopoly to Teleglobe for at least five years. Even were that to hold true, and there is nothing in this Bill that says it will, what will happen after the five years? There are employees of this company who have given 15 and 20 years of their life who, five years from now, will be working for a company that does not have that protection and that may not have the expertise or power to survive in a free market-place.
There is also the matter of security. As my colleague from Winnipeg-Birds Hill said, every country in the world depends on a secure communications system in that they own and operate to a certain extent their communications with other
countries of the world. When Britain sold its overseas telecommunication operations it retained 51 per cent and control remains under British direction. Almost every country in the world is in a similar situation with the exception of the U.S. However, the U.S. has a parallel system operated by the military which is as effective or maybe even more effective than the private system on which it only partially depends.
We are not only giving away a corporation which could do quite a bit to reduce the deficit over the next few years, but we are putting ourselves in the position where we will be dependent upon a corporation which may or may not make a profit. In the end it may have to divest itself of some of its less profitable operations.
There are a number of issues in this sale which the Government has not dealt with in the legislation. It has not taken care to make sure that the employees are satisfied with the new organization, not only for today but into the future. The Government has not made sure that the corporation will continue to be successful. The Government has not even ensured that it will be able to operate profitably beyond the first five years.
The Government has decided that privatization under any circumstances is a good thing. It came to office almost three years ago with the conviction that the privatization of Crown corporations was good for Government and the country. From the day it came into power it began to do something about that conviction. The experience of privatization has not proven that that conviction was worth while following. The Government is now privatizing with no consideration for public interest or public policy but rather on an ideological conviction which it does not even bother to defend.
Canadians must be very concerned about the idea that the Government should not be involved in any enterprise that can be operated by the private sector. There are many areas of service in the country which it makes a lot of sense for the Government to operate. Admittedly, there are many operations in which it does not make sense for the Government to be involved, but there is an area in between, and in that area each divestiture should be examined closely. The divestiture of Teleglobe is one which should have been examined carefully. Through this transaction we are putting into the hands of a private corporation part of an industry which is important, not only to us in Canada but in our relationships with other countries.
If the Government continues its commitment to privatization, we will eventually put at risk the basic structure of Canada. In the West, for instance, we have private telephone companies in almost every province and private hydro companies in every province. All those companies operate well. Those kinds of services as well as international telecommunication services should be carried out by the public sector. Consequently, we in this Party will not be able to support this Bill when it finally comes to a vote.
