subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS -MOTIONS   THE SENATE SUGGESTED EQUAL PROVINCIAL AND TERRITORIAL ELECTED REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is indeed an honour to speak to the motion of my colleague, the Hon. Member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor), with respect to abolishing the Senate and creating a new Senate. I believe this is a motion that is worthy of passage by this Parliament. I feel the best contribution I can make to the debate and, in particular, to Members who were elected in the election of 1984, is to reiterate the conclusions of the Special Joint Committee on Senate Reform on which I had the privilege to serve.
The special committee was composed of some eight Senators and ten Members of Parliament. We held hearings in Ottawa and in each provincial capital. We received and reviewed carefully some 280 briefs. We heard from 119 witnesses and some 30 organizations. We spent hundreds of hours reflecting on the issue. I now wish to read into the record part of the committee's conclusions. They are as follows:
We have concluded that the Canadian Senate should be elected directly by the people of Canada.
An appointed Senate no longer meets the needs of the Canadian federation. An elected Senate is the only kind of Senate that can adequately fill what we think should be its principal role-the role of regional representation. We propose a Senate different in composition and function from the House of Commons and from the present Senate. The second chamber we recommend is designed specifically-by its distribution of seats, by the way it is elected, and by the powers it exercises-to represent the sometimes diverse interests of the people of Canada's provinces and territories in federal legislation and federal policies.
In fulfilling that role, an elected Senate would strengthen the authority of Parliament to speak and act on behalf of Canadians in all parts of the country.
We reached this conclusion after reviewing the work of previous inquiries into the question of Senate reform and after hearing the testimony of witnesses in all provincial and territorial capitals ... We were told frequently that, after so many abortive attempts at Senate reform, the time has come for vigorous action-for fundamental change in the Senate-and that it would be a mistake to adopt inconsequential reforms.
Our conclusion was not reached lightly or easily. Although a substantial part of the testimony we heard favoured direct election, a roughly equal part opposed it, mainly on the grounds that a parliament with two elected houses cannot be reconciled comfortably with the principle of responsible government as it has operated in the British and Canadian traditions. Some highly respected people in public life and in the academic community prefer a reformed system of appointment to election. Among this group is one member of our Committee.
Although a reformed appointed Senate could bring about some needed improvements, we are persuaded that it would lack the political mandate to fill what we believe is the Senate's primary role. Only a politically strong second chamber can dispute, when necessary, the decisions taken by a government that is supported by the House of Commons.
Therefore only an elected Senate can satisfy the original intent of the Fathers of Confederation: the provision of a chamber that would balance judiciously the power of the Commons (which is based on representation by population) by safeguarding the legitimate interests of the people of the less populous provinces-
We believe that Canada should establish an elected Senate designed in such a way that it would not be vying continually for supremacy with the House of Commons: it should have significant powers, but it should not be able to undermine Canada's well-tried system of responsible government. We therefore propose that the new Senate be given only a suspensive veto, which would allow time for national debate and reflection, but which the Commons

March 30, 1987
The Senate
could, after a suitable lapse of time, override by re-passing the legislation in question.
We also propose that every effort be made to ensure that Senators have a significant degree of independence of party. Only then will they be able to speak in favour of local and regional interests without having to be concerned primarily, as Members of Parliament must be, with adhering to party policy. A healthy measure of independence is therefore essential if the Senate is to fill its role of regional representation. This does not mean that Senators would lose sight of the needs of the country as a whole.
It is for this reason, and also to distinguish Senators from members of the House of Commons, we propose that Senators be elected for a single but comparatively long term-nine years-with one-third of the Senators being elected every three years.
To lessen party influence in the choice of Senators, all but one of us prefer 'first-past-the-post' elections in single-member constituencies to proportional representation in multi-member constituencies. Each province would be divided into as many constituencies as it had Senators.
We recognize that, in the absence of proportional representation for an elected Senate, the political parties will have to work hard to achieve balanced representation from across the country in the Commons and the Senate. This is as it should be. In striving to do this, they will have to adopt their policies accordingly, and this can only benefit national politics.
On the question of the distribution of seats, the Committee was advised by nearly all witnesses across Canada that the division should be made not on the basis of the present four Senate regions but by allocating seats to each province and territory. We accept that this kind of allocation reflects more closely the diverse nature of Canada.
As to how many seats should be allocated to each province or territory, we recognize that there is no perfect solution. We believe that giving an equal number of seats to each province would not be appropriate, having regard to Canada's historical development and the configuration of its population. If each province had the same number of seats, five provinces with as little as 13.4 per cent of Canada's population would have a majority of seats if they had the support of the territories.
While the less populous provinces merit a stronger voice in Parliament, equal representation in the Senate would tilt the balance too far and would be unacceptable to the vast majority of Canadians, not only to those living in the two largest provinces. We therefore propose a compromise whereby most provinces would have an equal number of seats, but Ontario and Quebec would have more and Prince Edward Island and the territories would have fewer. Our proposal would, for example, give the four western provinces together as many seats as Ontario and Quebec jointly. We believe that most Canadians would agree that our proposed distribution, or something close to it, represents a fair solution.
That quotation gives the heart and core of the summary of a thoughtful committee composed of some eight Senators and some 10 Members of Parliament which studied 280 briefs and held hearings in every province of Canada. I personally believe that a combination of this report, together with the report of the Alberta Legislature done by the committee chaired by Dennis Anderson, who is now the Minister of Culture for the Province of Alberta, would give a solid basis for reform of the Senate, something which I think we all agree is very much needed. Elowever, I think western Canadians in particular have to consider carefully the question of "equal per province" since I am not sure that in a resource-based economy it would be wise in the long term for us to transfer to five provinces with only 13.4 per cent of the population a majority of Senate seats. That constitutes a very serious question that I have with respect to the Triple E proposal. It is something that I would join with in a flash if it could satisfactorily answer the question of the transfer of power to one region.
The federal report proposed that there be 96 Senators representing the regions, with 48 seats for the two populous provinces: Ontario would keep 24, Quebec would keep 24. The four western provinces would have 48 seats, thereby neutralizing the two central provinces; and the Atlantic region and the Territories would have 48 seats.
That would amount to a massive transfer of power to the regions, at the Senate level. I believe that is a proper transfer of power, and it is one that Ontario and Quebec could live with as compared to the current Triple E proposal, which calls for an equal number of Senate seats for the provinces.
As Members consider this question, I hope that they will take these views into consideration.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS -MOTIONS   THE SENATE SUGGESTED EQUAL PROVINCIAL AND TERRITORIAL ELECTED REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the motion before the House today, presented by the Hon. Member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor), urges the Government to consider introducing the appropriate measures to create an elected Senate where provinces and territories will enjoy equal representation.
An elected Senate and equal representation for the provinces reflect the proposals submitted and supported by various groups and individuals, including the Premier of the province represented by the mover of this motion. I would like to point out, however, that most proponents of an elected Senate have a third requirement in addition to the two "e's" of "elected" and "equality". They would like to see effectiveness in the Upper House, Mr. Speaker.
I think it would be useful to take a few moments to consider how effective a reformed Senate could be. When we make any changes in the powers of the Senate, such changes also affect the powers of the House of Commons and its ability to defend the interests of the people. Among the proposals for Senate reform, made in the last decade, four major reform proposals recommended having an elected Senate. These proposals were submitted by the Canada West Foundation in 1981, by the Government of Prince Edward Island in 1983, by a Special Joint Committee of Parliament in 1984, which was referred to by the previous Speaker, and last but not least, a plan was proposed by a committee of the Alberta Legislature in March 1985 and renewed since by the Premier of that province.
Of these four plans, only one did not propose electing the same number of senators from each province. The Special Joint Committee of the House of Commons and the Senate was more in favour of a weighting system that would encourage over-representation of the smaller provinces while nevertheless respecting substantial differences in population. According to the report, this formula would prevent five provinces with only 13.4 per cent of the population from controlling the Senate or one inhabitant of Prince Edward Island from being the equivalent of 70 Ontarians or 50 Quebecers for the purposes of representation in the Upper House.
March 30, 1987

Committee members recommended that the Provinces of Ontario and Quebec should be represented by 24 senators each, Prince Edward Island by six and the other provinces by 12 each.
To respect the statutory equality of each component of the Canadian federation and ensure that national policy takes into consideration the interests of outlying regions, proposals by the Canada West Foundation and the Governments of Prince Edward Island and Alberta, as well as the motion by the Hon. Member for Bow River, all fall back on the formula applied in the United States, in Switzerland and Australia, with the request that the provinces be represented in the Senate on an equal basis.
However, where the motion by the Hon. Member for Bow River is silent on the question of the powers of a reformed Senate, the three proposals I mentioned earlier do focus on this question.
In a study made in 1983, the Government of Prince Edward Island suggested that a Senate elected on the basis of provincial equality should retain the full legislative powers possessed by the Senate as we know it today. Although it would not, and it does not today, have the power to initiate supply Bills, the Senate would retain its absolute veto over all measures adopted by the House of Commons and would, generally speaking, exercise the same powers as the House of Commons.
According to the document submitted by Prince Edward Island, Senate reform would not be justified if that body were to be deprived of the necessary powers to defend the interests of those it is supposed to represent.
In 1981, the Canada West Foundation also proposed that on the basis of its increased legitimacy, an elected Senate should be able to maintain its right to vote on Bills initiated by the House of Commons and to exercise substantial powers.
According to this project the basis of representation-the population for the Commons and the province for the Senate- did not justify one House being directly subordinated to the other. The consensus was that allowing the Senate to have its say about ordinary legislation would guarantee that regional views would be taken under consideration in drafting national policies. However the Canada West Foundation did not go as far as giving the Senate a veto over ordinary legislation. Deadlocks would be impossible since a legislative measure rejected by the Senate would come into force after reendorsement by a significant Commons majority. Without actually specifying the terms, the proposition made it clear that in most cases a significant majority would imply that the Government in office would seek the support of some of the Opposition Members to reverse a Senate vote.
But the Senate would have an absolute veto in cases of constitutional amendments to ratify certain appointments and to authorize the Government of Canada to exercise such extraordinary powers as war measures, disallowance and declaratory powers.
The Senate
In short, the Canada West Foundation position in 1981 was that the Senate would be effective in the sense that the Upper House would be able to examine and amend all Bills, exercise a power of suspensive veto over most pieces of legislation, and of absolute veto over extraordinary Government measures.
In 1985, the Special Committee of the Alberta Legislature also looked at the question of the Senate's effectiveness. It recommended that the Senate retain the power it now has to discuss and recommend amendments to all the Bills coming from the House of Commons. The Senate would still have the right to oppose legislation, but the House would have various ways of getting around that opposition.
On constitutional matters, the Senate's veto would only be suspensive for a period of 180 days, as the 1982 constitutional Act now provides. A negative vote by the Senate on legislation with financial or tax implications could be overturned by a simple majority vote here in the Commons.
Finally, on all non-financial Bills, a Senate amendment or veto could only be overturned in the Commons by a larger majority vote than that expressed in the Senate.
Honourable Members will have understood from the foregoing that proponents of the Triple E-Senate support significant powers for Senators. Their view is that the Senate's effectiveness in defending regional interests requires that it be able to control, if not direct, natural policies.
Maintaining the current veto, as proposed by Prince Edward Island, or the requirement of an outlandish majority in the Commons to go around a negative vote in the Senate, are only two of the possible means of strengthening the higher Chamber to make it more effective.
The need for such effectiveness is indeed clear. Once elected, the Senate would have the legitimacy it now lacks to exercise its broad powers. To that new legitimacy, equal provincial representation will add a clear mandate by indicating to the Senate what interests it must protect.
Knowing the commitment of Canadians to their regions, a chamber that would be devoted solely to the defence of provinces would not be long in gaining their sympathy, thereby strengthening its mandate. Therefore, how could we deny that legitimate chamber the powers required by its mandate? There would be no reason to do so. This is what supporters of the Triple-E Senate formula have understood.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to stress that for some time already, one of my constituents, Mr. Jean-Guy Legault, from Oka, who chairs the Fondation Edouard- Mont petit, has been consistantly asking the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) to appoint volunteer deputy senators whose responsibility would be to advise the Government on draft Bills, etc. While finding this proposal original-it clearly goes against the reported collective will of an elected Senate-I am convinced that Mr. Legault will be interested in today's debate which will give him the opportunity to add new elements to his proposal or amend some current ones.

March 30, 1987
The Senate
At the same time, Mr. Speaker, I will send him a copy of today's Debates. I see that you're indicating to me that I may still have a minute and a half left.
With equal powers and different representation structures, would the two Chambers not run the risk of attracting sympathy from different segments of the population, thereby increasing the opportunities for conflicts?
Although the supporters of an elected Senate have convinced me of the validity of their claims and a need for reform, none as yet has reassured me as to the dominant role the House of Commons would continue to play. To these and similar questions which come to mind today I have not yet found any completely satisfactory answer. It seems to me that, so far, the issue of Senate reform has been addressed in isolation, independently from the development of other Government institutions.
Without opposing this reform, Mr. Speaker, I feel that we should look into its impact on our political life generally, and of course I would fully support unreservedly any initiative to that end.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS -MOTIONS   THE SENATE SUGGESTED EQUAL PROVINCIAL AND TERRITORIAL ELECTED REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I begin my contribution to the debate as I did on a previous motion by the Hon. Member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Parry). His Private Member's motion called for the abolition of the Senate by calling to the attention of Hon. Members the traditional or long held view of the New Democratic Party of Canada that the Senate ought to be abolished because of its non-democratic nature.
However, I want to make clear that it is the current nondemocratic Senate which my Party has a long-standing policy of wanting to abolish. In my judgment there is openness within the Party, collectively and among individual New Democrats, on what kind of democratic Senate might be appropriately put in the place of the current non-democratic Senate which, as I said, ought to be abolished.
One of the origins of the current push for Senate reform quite legitimately comes from the feeling of certain regions in Canada that they do not have enough power at the centre, that they do not have enough power in the decision-making process in Ottawa, whether it is in the House of Commons or in the Senate as it now stands. They feel that there is a strong tendency, manifest in many ways, for the decision-making process in the House of Commons not to take into consideration the interest of the regions. I speak particularly from the point of view of the region from which I come, that is, western Canada.
Another way people have thought about addressing the problem has been through House of Commons reforms. They have imagined ways in which, through a combination of the system we have now, proportional representation, and representation based upon regions as opposed to constituencies
strictly, we might be able to address the imbalance between the centre and the periphery in the House of Commons and still be able to get rid of the Senate and have a unicameral House.
That is not what we are debating today. We are debating the motion of the Hon. Member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor) which, as I understand it, calls for a Triple E Senate. It is important that these kinds of motions have come forward because they give us a chance to debate the matter. I am particularly appreciative of the contribution of the Hon. Member for Lethbridge-Foothills (Mr. Thacker) who I think did the House a service by reading into the record the recommendations of the Joint Committee on Senate Reform. He pointed to the fact, if I understood him correctly, that the notion of equality could be achieved, not necessarily on a province-by-province basis, but on the same sort of regional basis originally envisioned in the constitutional amending formula at one point, where we would have had western Canada considered as a region, Ontario considered as a region, Quebec considered as a region, and Atlantic Canada considered as a region. If we had equal representation devised on that basis, we might then get over some of the problems involved in having equal representation from each province. I think that bears more study.
However, one thing which concerns me as a western Canadian is some of the expectations raised around the idea of a Triple E Senate and what it could do. Part of the problem with the Triple E Senate proposal is that we do not know exactly what powers many of its advocates have in mind, whether it would be strictly a suspensive power, whether it would have well defined areas of jurisdiction, et cetera.
There is a variety of expectations being placed upon the Triple E Senate. In my judgment, support for such a Senate, although I respect many of the people who advocate it, has come into rather bad company lately with the support being given to it by an editorial in the Western Report by Mr. Ted Byfield. He went on at great length giving, in my judgment, the classic example of the false expectations raised about a Triple E Senate.
He referred back to the controversy over the CF-18 contract. He suggested that had there been a debate in the new Triple E Senate which he had in mind, these new Senators, unbound by Party discipline, would have somehow been able to prevent the decision to give the CF-18 contract to Montreal instead of to Winnipeg where it should have gone.
He used the phrase, "Unlike the Commons debate, it would be worth covering". As you know, Mr. Speaker, and as everyone knows, there was no Commons debate on the CF-18 contract. It was a contract let by the Government with the full powers of the Government. There was no debate in the Commons. There would not be such a debate in any new Senate, except in some aside way, the same way as we managed to have an aside debate in the House of Commons during Question Period about the contract after the fact.
March 30, 1987

There would have been no debate either in the Commons or in a Triple E Senate on a matter of government contracts.
It is quite misleading to give the impression that somehow a Triple E Senate would have been able to stop that or that a Triple E Senate would somehow exist in some sort of pristine political atmosphere where Parties would not have any effect.
I remind Mr. Byfield, through you, Mr. Speaker, that it was the Tory Premiers of western Canada-and Mr. Byfield is fond of chastising New Democratic Members of Parliament from western Canada-who decided not to stand by the Premier of Manitoba, Mr. Pawley, in his protestation against the CF-18 contract going to Montreal. They certainly had more freedom than any Senator would have had down here, working in close proximity to the Government. Yet, they could not be prevailed upon, through any sense of western Canadian solidarity, to be more than purely symbolic in their solidarity with Manitoba in protesting the injustice of the contract going to Montreal.
I think the whole debate about a Triple E Senate insofar as it relates to western alienation is being poisoned by this kind of false expectation. I think it is being done deliberately. I should like to quote from the March 16 editorial. It says:
Unlike the Commons debate, it would be worth covering. Neither in the
Senate would we have to witness such loathsome spectacles as that of four
Manitoba NDP members declaring themselves in favour of taking the CF-18
project away from their own province.
You were here, Mr. Speaker, in the fall of 1986, as were the Hon. Member for Lethbridge-Foothills, the Hon. Member for Brandon-Souris (Mr. Clark), and many others. They will know-and I hope everyone will agree with me-that it is simply a lie, just a lie to say that we, the NDP Members of Parliament from Manitoba, declared ourselves in favour of taking the CF-18 project away from our own province. Why would anyone want to say that when it is so patently untrue, and say it twice?
This kind of thing was said previously in the Western Report, and I wrote a letter to the editor which was printed. Subsequent to that, a month or so later, we get, in the form of this editorial, a blatant lie.
This was raised in the House many times by Manitoban New Democratic Members of Parliament. If Mr. Byfield, or anyone else for that matter, is unhappy about the way the House of Commons works or the way the New Democratic Party handled the CF-18 contract, there are many criticisms he could make, but there is one thing he could not say with any pretension to truthfulness, namely, that the four Manitoba New Democratic Members of Parliament were in favour of the contract going to Montreal.
This debate has become tied to a much more serious political reality in western Canada. It has become associated with a deliberate attempt on the part of certain elements in western Canada, Mr. Byfield among them, to distort and misrepresent what is actually going on here in the House of
The Senate
Commons. There is enough to be unhappy about in terms of real western alienation and western Canadian grievances. I would be the first one to admit that. We ought not, for obviously ideological reasons, pretend that certain things happen when they did not happen. We ought not to allow people like Mr. Byfield to pretend that the only real western Canadians are those who happen to agree with him. We western Canadians disagree among ourselves, be we New Democrats or Progressive Conservative western Canadians. We have had left-wing Governments and right-wing Governments, and we do all that within the freedom of the democratic process that we cherish. For anyone, Mr. Byfield or anyone else, to pretend that somehow only those who agree with the Western Report are real western Canadians is a disservice not only to New Democrats, whom he is so fond of attacking, but also to Progressive Conservative Members of Parliament from Alberta and from western Canada generally who are now becoming the object of this particular form of garbage journalism.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS -MOTIONS   THE SENATE SUGGESTED EQUAL PROVINCIAL AND TERRITORIAL ELECTED REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to take part in the debate on the motion presented by the Hon. Member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor), which seeks the abolition of the Senate and the creation of a new Senate composed of Senators elected by the people on the basis of equal representation for each province and territory. The motion also urges the Government to initiate intergovernmental discussions to that end at the earliest opportunity.
Today I would like to take a closer look at one of the most interesting aspects of Senate reform, a subject that has been getting a great deal of attention recently in this House.
Mr. Speaker, when we look at the purpose or objective of the Senate reform, I think we should look at the various roles that could be played by a new Upper House. 1 think it would be useful to consider the function of the Upper House, especially in other countries with a federal system. In most cases, the Upper House has a responsibility for examining legislation. It is supposed to look at legislative measures to detect any possible errors, contradictions or shortcomings. Today, most Upper Houses perform this function without challenging the general principles or policies underlying legislation already adopted by the Lower House. Often, they are also asked to provide legislative support. For instance, Upper Houses may conduct inquiries on questions of public policy or they may have special powers to scrutinize subordinate legislation.
Some Upper Houses play a role in representing and protecting minorities. When minorities are regrouped geographically in a given region, they can be protected from the majority by giving this region a specially weighted representation. During the debate prior to Confederation, Lower Canada demanded representation in the Senate equal to that of the two other regions, Ontario and the Maritimes, and it is clear that the francophone leaders at the time thus hoped to enjoy a form

March 30, 1987
The Senate
of linguistic and cultural protection. Mr. Speaker, there is also the option of demanding special procedures when voting on certain issues in the Upper House, so as to avoid any hasty action that might prove prejudicial to the interests or rights of certain minorities.
Upper Houses can have an intergovernmental function. They can be structured to enable various governments within a federation to take part in the business of the central or federal Government. A prime example of this is the Bundesrat in West Germany, whose members are Ministers or their delegates of the Governments of the component States. Members of the Bundesrat vote as one according to the instructions given by their respective governments. Many observers think that the Bundesrat makes an appreciable contribution to intergovernmental coordination and cooperation within Western Germany. In the late 70s the supporters of Senate reform in Canada came up with a number of propositions aimed at creating a similar institution at the federal level.
The fourth function which a second chamber may have is to represent the regions. This is intended to mean representation of the regions or constituent elements on a basis other than representation by population. In certain cases each state or province may have a representation equal to the second chamber. In others the number of members may vary, but the scale is usually tipped in favour of those with fewer people. In any case it is always a matter of limiting somewhat the will of the Lower House by reflecting the diversity of the regions or elements which make up the federation and, to that extent, to compensate for the rule of simple majority.
It is widely acknowledged that the first and second of these four functions-examining legislation and representing regions-are the ones which were expected to be the main role of the Senate when it was created. In light of this we can indeed wonder about the way the Senate has fulfilled these functions over the years. To answer the question, I would refer to the report of the Special Joint Committee of the Senate and of the House of Commons which was tabled in the House in January 1984.
According to the report, the role of the Senate had evolved so as to complement rather than compete with the popularly elected House of Commons. The Committee made the following comments concerning the role of the existing Senate, and I quote:
Its principal functions are now improving legislation and investigating questions of public policy. It is said that investigation is one area where the present Senate has shown a commendable degree of independence from the executive.
On the matter of other important functions the Senate could perform, the Committee report noted that:
The more recent arguments for Senate reform-notably those made to our Committee-have focused on achieving one of the original goals of the Senate, the protection and representation of regional interests. These arguments spring from a belief that Parliament needs a chamber that represents those interests with more political authority that can be achieved with a Senate appointed in the present way.
Based on the representations made by the various witnesses, the Committee went on to say:
The principal complaint the Committee encountered was that federal institutions as they are now constructed are unable to express and mediate regional concerns. Although the Senate was originally designed to give the regions a weighted voice in Parliament's decisions, it is argued that this does not apply. Witnesses pointed out that regional interests are now forced to seek outlets through other means, often through provincial governments.
It is very clear, Mr. Speaker, in the Committee's report, that most witnesses heard focussed on the Senate's representational role. For instance, Hon. Robert Stanfield expressed the following opinion:
I find it highly desirable that we have a Senate that would allow regions to be more present and have more influence in Ottawa.
I do not believe it is possible to govern this country in a satisfactory manner based only on the majority rule, in spite of the distribution of powers and the Charter of Rights.
For its part, the Business Council on National Issues noted the following:
The specific powers that should be vested in a new, elective Higher Chamber are less important than the principle that there must be an elected Canadian Senate, and that it should play a positive and strong role to iron out increasing regional tensions.
In its report, the Committee recognized that better regional representation was important in the opinion of witnesses.
The principal complaint the Committee encountered was that federal institutions as they are now constructed are unable to express and mediate regional concerns ... The more recent arguments for Senate reform-have focused on achieving one of the original goals of the Senate: the protection and representation of regional interests.
The Committee further emphasized that its primary objective was
-to strengthen the Senate's capacity to fill its role of regional representation. If this objective and others which are consequential were achieved, there would be a new forum whose principal role would be to discuss openly and to reconcile competing regional interests in matters under federal jurisdiction. We do not argue that regional differences would disappear, but we do believe that the system for resolving them would be much improved and that regional tensions would be less troublesome-
Similar arguments could be found in a fairly recent study on the Senate reform. In its report issued in March 1985, the Alberta Legislative Assembly's Special Committee on the reform of the Senate wrote, and I quote:
The role of an Upper Chamber in the federal decision-making process is effectively quite clear. The first function of the Canadian Senate, as contemplated by the Fathers of Confederation, was to represent provincial points of view within the federal decision-making process. The Committee does not believe that the Senate should get involved in intergovernment negotiations. The Senate of Canada must have, as its first objective, to continue representing regions at the federal level, as the Fathers of Confederation wanted it.
In the light of the few examples I have just given, Mr. Speaker, it can be said that the recent proposals aimed at reforming the Senate all share a common objective: To improve regional representation within the Senate and Parliament as a whole. I feel that during our discussions on the way to improve the Senate's regional representation, we should keep in mind that, basically, it is the Canadian people which will make it possible for the Senate to become a truly efficient
March 30, 1987

forum; through their support for a reformed Senate, whatever its nature, it will receive the power to act on behalf of the regions during the proceedings of Parliament.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS -MOTIONS   THE SENATE SUGGESTED EQUAL PROVINCIAL AND TERRITORIAL ELECTED REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this resolution before the House is two-pronged. The first part is very easy to support. It calls on us to abolish the Senate as it is today. I support that because I believe the Senate as we know it today is an affront to democracy. Senators are appointed until age 75. They are not elected and they are responsible to no one once appointed. Neither can they be recalled.
The second part of the resolution is a bit trickier. It suggests that we create a new Senate composed of Senators elected by the people of Canada on the basis of equal representation for each province and territory, and to initiate discussions to that end with provincial and territorial Governments at the earliest opportunity.
Speaking only for myself, I believe we should initiate some discussion on the possibility of an elected Senate. There should be some discussion as to the kind of representation we want in the other place, if any at all. I hesitate to endorse the idea of a Triple-E Senate as proposed in this motion by the Hon. Member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor) because it says that there should be equal representation for each province and territory. I am concerned that because we have so many small provinces and territories with very small populations there could be a time when a majority of Senators represent less than 10 per cent of the population of Canada. For example, if one were to have 10 Senators per province or territory, or five, you could add the populations of the four Atlantic provinces, Yukon and the Northwest Territories, and that would be half the Senate, and they would represent less than 10 per cent of the population of Canada. I think that is going a bit too far.
On the other hand, I think it is extremely important in a federal democratic state that there be a balance between representation by population on the one side and representation by region on the other. There has to be some balance between the two. We do not have that balance today. Ontario and Quebec make up the overwhelming majority of our population, about 38 per cent in Ontario and about 28 per cent in Quebec. Add those figures, and you will find that two-thirds of the Canadian population lives in two provinces. As a result, this House of Commons is dominated by those two provinces under representation by population.
We have to find some way of balancing that with representation by region. The Hon. Member for Lethbridge-Foothills (Mr. Thacker) talked about equal representation from each region. That is one possible way of doing it. The system would perhaps allow for special recognition of Quebec and the French fact. Perhaps there should be some special recognition of our native people on matters affecting their rights where a majority of native Senators would agree with the rest. Those
The Senate
are things we could look at in considering the possibility of another place.
I want to indicate my support for the idea of looking at taking steps in this direction without endorsing all the ideas in a Triple-E Senate. It is very important that we have some representation by region as well as by population. For example, in the U.S. House of Representatives there is representation by population. A state like North Dakota has one Congressman, as does the small state of Rhode Island. New York and California have many Congressmen and Congresswomen because of the size of their populations. On the other hand, there is representation by region in the Senate where every state gets two Senators, whether it be Rhode Island, North Dakota, New York or California. The U.S. has that balance, which I think is so important.
We of course now recognize equality of the provinces in our amending formula. To amend the Constitution you need to have agreement by at least seven provinces and they must represent at least 50 per cent of the population. That covers both regions and populations and gives us that balance which is so important.
Going back to the U.S., there is no way that a number of smaller states could block the will of the country as a whole. We could have that kind of situation here where the smaller provinces and the territories, with about 8 per cent of the population, would have as many Senators as the rest of the country and its 92 per cent of the population. That does not exist in the U.S. because there are many more states of roughly equal size, many more states of moderate size, and many more states of small size. There is that difference in the two systems.
I would like to return to the first part of the motion, which is to abolish the Senate. As I said, I believe the present Senate is not a democratic institution. It is an affront to democracy, a throwback to the 19th century. I believe that the Senate, as it exists today, should be abolished. I think all Members of Parliament should agree to that. I have nothing whatsoever against any member of the other place. There are many fine men and women who are Senators in the other place who work very hard and have served this country very well. However, in many ways the other place has become a house of patronage. Many people who worked very hard for the Prime Minister's Party, regardless of what it may be, got their just reward by being appointed there until the age of 75, regardless of whether or not they work or keep in touch with the province which they represent.
The second thing that concerns me is that campaign managers are appointed to the other place by the Prime Minister, regardless of his Party. They have a public office, draw a large salary, and have a large expense account and a staff paid for by the public. A good example is Senator Atkins who was appointed by the present Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney). Senator Jean Bazin is there in the same capacity.

March 30, 1987
The Senate
On the Liberal side there is Senator Keith Davey, a good friend of mine who has been there for many, many years. He is the chief Liberal campaign manager in the country extending back to the days of Lester Pearson. Senator Kirby is the newer version of Senator Keith Davey. He is a very intelligent man, a very decent Canadian, and a very competent political manager. However, that is not the role of the Senate. In a democratic society people should not be appointed for such functions in such an institution. I believe campaign managers should be paid out of the coffers of political Parties rather than by the people of Canada. That is not the purpose for which the Senate was created. That is another reason that the Senate of Canada, in its present state, should be abolished.
With that I call upon the House to support the first part of this motion to abolish the Senate. Although I do not agree with everything that has been advocated with regard to a Triple E Senate, I believe we should study this motion and begin discussions as soon as possible with regard to whether or not there should be an elected second House in this country in order to have a balance between "rep by pop" and "rep by regionalism". Without that, in a federal state we will have continuing problems of disunity within all political Parties because the problems of central Canada are often perceived as being more important than those of the west, the north, or Atlantic Canada.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS -MOTIONS   THE SENATE SUGGESTED EQUAL PROVINCIAL AND TERRITORIAL ELECTED REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think no one in this House can doubt the necessity of doing something about the other place. Since the September, 1984 election, Members of this House have witnessed two incidents where Members of the other place have sought to frustrate the will of this House. With this in mind I would draw the attention of Hon. Members to the serious conflict at the turn of the century between the British House of Lords and the House of Commons, which culminated in the Parliament Act of 1911. I would like to take a few moments to explore the development of the Act because it is important in terms of the discussion which we are presently having.
The real catalyst of that crisis was the 1909 Budget of Mr. Lloyd George, Chancellor of the Exchequer. He, like the Government of Canada today, faced the problem of a large deficit and introduced a series of taxation measures which particularly affected Britain's wealthy land-owning class. Some observers at the time suggested that the Liberal Government had brought forward a particularly tough Budget in order to dare the Lords to veto it, thus allowing the Liberals to go to the electorate on a "peers versus the people" platform. Whether or not that is true, the fact remains that the Lords had not rejected a finance Bill in 250 years.
On November 30, 1909, the House of Lords rejected the Budget and in doing so disregarded one of the most fundamental principles of the parliamentary system, that is that the power of the purse belongs to the democratically elected House of Commons alone. Parliament was then dissolved and, as expected, both the Budget and the unparalleled action of the Lords were the key election issues. The Liberals remained in
power with the support of a group of Irish nationalists who demanded that limits be put on the power of the Lords.
The Liberals then began to draft the Parliament Bill. It was introduced on April 15, and the 1909 Budget was passed without incident by both Chambers a few days later. With the introduction of the Parliament Bill came a warning from Prime Minister Asquith that if the Lords rejected the Bill there would not only be a second election, but the existence of the House of Lords would be an election issue.
A constitutional conference of Liberal and Unionist Party leaders aimed at ending the crisis was quickly convened. That went on from June until November when Prime Minister Asquith finally admitted that there was "an apparently irreconcilable divergence of opinion" between the two Parties. Shortly thereafter, in an audience with King George V, Asquith sought a guarantee that, assuming a Liberal victory in a general election, enough Liberal peers would be created to allow the passage of the Parliament Bill in the event of another deadlock. This guarantee was obtained.
As expected, the December, 1910, general election produced another stalemate, but Balfour himself, who had urged his House of Lords colleagues to reject the Bill in the first place, recognized that the British public had had enough and that the Unionists ran the risk of being blamed for any further constitutional upheaval.
After a serious and emotion-filled debate in both Houses, the Parliament Bill was finally passed on August 11, 1911. The vote in the House of the Lords was 131 to 114, with 37 Unionists voting with the Government. As you are aware, Mr. Speaker, the Parliament Act seriously reduced the power of the Lords. If the House of Lords does not pass a money Bill certified as such by you, Sir, the Speaker, within 30 days of its passage by the Commons, it may be presented for assent without the Lords' consent. In 1949 the Lords' power to prevent or unduly delay the passage of legislation was reduced still further. The Parliament Act has rightly been described as the most decisive step in British constitutional history since the extension of the franchise in 1867. It greatly reduced the authority of the House of Lords and established once and for all the supremacy of the democratically elected House of Commons in our parliamentary system.
I think you will see from my recounting of these events, Mr. Speaker, the similarity to the situation we face regarding the Canadian Senate. Here, too, there have been attempts by the majority Party in that Chamber, an appointed, non-accountable body, to thwart the clearly-expressed wishes of the House of Commons. Not only that, but the first incident was on a question involving public revenues, which are indeed the responsibility of the people's representatives in this House. Just as the "ditchers" of 1911 refused to accept the decision of the majority, we, too, have witnessed vain efforts from our own little band of "ditchers".
George Dangerfield, in his book, The Strange Death of Liberal England, put the matter very well. He said that these
March 30, 1987

individuals "did not realize that life consists in change, that nothing can stand still.... Clinging to the realities of the past, they prepared to defend their dead cause to the finish".
I sincerely hope, Mr. Speaker, that all Hon. Members, both here and in the other place, will heed the words of Dangerfield.

ENVIRONMENTAL AFFAIRS-POSSIBLE USE OF LOW-SULPHUR WESTERN COAL BY ONTARIO HYDRO
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, you are probably not aware of it, but I have a friend and constituent by the name of Judy Fournier. Judy lives in my constituency in the Don Mills Road and Lawrence Avenue area.
She has a brother who works for a coal company in Grande Cache, Alberta. This coal company used to be very prosperous. Its sales were very high, but recently they have gone down, production has fallen, and there have been lay-offs, as I am sure you are aware. The fact that there have been lay-offs at this mine in Grande Cache, Alberta, is an example of the problems that the Alberta economy has been facing and an example of the problems of regional economic disparity in Canada.
As you know, jobs are available in Toronto and, in fact, a report in the newspaper on the weekend states that thousands of jobs are unfilled at the moment. However, there is unemployment in Alberta and elsewhere in Canada. Judy Fournier is worried about her brother and his future. Although he has been working at that mine for a long time, even with his seniority he may very well be out of a job before too long.
Judy has a boss who is a very good friend of mine. His name is Chuck Thornton. He owns a printing company in Toronto
Adjournment Debate
and he and his family also have a cottage property on an island in Lake Muskoka near Gravenhurst, Ontario. It is a beautiful cottage, on a beautiful lake, in a beautiful summer resort area.
That summer resort area, Lake Muskoka, and the Muskoka Lakes generally, have a problem. The problem is acid rain. There is an answer to that problem, an answer to Judy Fournier's problem, and an answer to the problem facing Chuck Thornton and his family. The answer, which is the same, is for Ontario Hydro to begin using low-sulphur western coal instead of the high-sulphur American coal it is now using to generate electric power.
The House will know that a study was completed last summer which indicated that if Ontario would begin substituting western coal for U.S. coal, it could create some 13,000 permanent jobs until the year 2000. Most of those jobs would be created in Alberta and British Columbia and perhaps as much as 40 per cent would be created in Ontario.
That same study indicated that the income that would be generated by that effort would be some $4.1 billion. Of course, that would be important for western Canada and Canada as a whole, and, perhaps from a parochial point of view, it would be important for Ontario because it would cut the amount of acid rain emissions and reduce the amount of acid rain in Ontario.
As you know, Mr. Speaker, and as the Parliamentary Secretary knows, Ontario has agreed to cut its acid rain emissions by some 50 per cent by 1994. Ontario Hydro is responsible, through its coal and thermal generating plants, for some 85 per cent to 90 per cent of all of those emissions. Western coal, on the other hand, has a sulphur level of 0.25 per cent compared to the U.S. coal-sulphur level of 2.2 per cent.
If Ontario Hydro would use Canadian coal instead of American coal, it would create jobs, it would reduce regional economic disparity, it would help bind our country together instead of tearing it apart, and it would reduce acid rain emissions in Ontario. It would reduce acid rain which would help our lakes, fish, birds, trees and people with respiratory problems. It would make Judy Fournier happy. It would make Judy's brother happy. It would make my friend, Chuck Thornton, happy, and his entire family, his wife Pam and his children, Scott, Bruce and Paul, would all be happy. It would make the people of Ontario happy and it would make the people of Canada happy.
What is holding it up? Of course, it is Ontario Hydro and it is the Ontario Government. I ask you, Premier Peterson, what is holding it up? Let us get on with it. Let us substitute western coal for U.S. coal. Let us create some jobs and cut acid rain in Ontario.

speakeroldname: Mr. Doug Lewis (Parliamentary Secretary to Deputy Prime Minister and President of the Privy Council):
subtopic: ENVIRONMENTAL AFFAIRS-POSSIBLE USE OF LOW-SULPHUR WESTERN COAL BY ONTARIO HYDRO
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to compliment my colleague on his continued interest in environmental matters, especially acid rain. I want

March 30, 1987
Adjournment Debate
to lend my voice to his efforts to encourage Ontario Hydro to use western coal.
My colleague asked the Deputy Prime Minister if the Premier of Ontario is prepared to order Ontario Hydro to cut acid rain emissions in the same manner that private industry has been asked. The Deputy Prime Minister has met with the Premiers of Ontario, Saskatchewan, Alberta and British Columbia to seek ways to use low-sulphur western Canadian coal at Ontario Hydro. This is in response to the federal-provincial task force which reported in June of 1986 and recommended that increased utilization of western coal be treated not just as a possibility but, indeed, as a reality. Not only is this possible from a financial sense, but its importance in reducing acid rain is the key concern.
The sulphur content of western Canadian coal is .3 per cent. This is about nine times less than the sulphur content of Pennsylvania coal. That is the reason we must take advantage of our western-Canadian coal. The Hon. Member asks whether Ontario Hydro has been ordered to reduce its acid gas emissions in the future. The short answer to this is, yes. In fact, Ontario Hydro has pledged to reduce its total acid gas emissions by 50 per cent over the next six years. This means that the 430,000 tonnes per year of acid gas emissions must be reduced to less than 215,000 tonnes per year by 1994.
In order to reach this level it is anticipated that during the 1990s, when Ontario Hydro will be needing new capacity, western-Canadian coal will be efficiently utilized to ensure these levels are met. This project could potentially create 13,000 jobs across Canada.
That is the reason we are treating it as an exciting project which will unite the country and will provide jobs in many regions and reduce acid rain. Quite clearly, this is good for the economy, good for the environment, good for Ontario, good for the western provinces and, Mr. Speaker, good for Canada. We are very optimistic that this project will become a reality in the near future.

Mr. Speaker, on March 5, 1987, I rose in this House to ask a question of the Solicitor General (Mr. Kelleher) about the steps being taken to combat the problem of illiteracy among prisoners. My question was prompted by the discovery of some alarming statistics.
Before pursuing my specific question about the illiteracy rates in prison, I would like to comment on this problem, which exists throughout our entire society. By coincidence, the leading editorial of The Globe and Mail today provides some shocking statistics about the illiteracy afflicting many Canadians.
Some one million Canadians cannot read at all, and four million cannot read or write well enough to function adequately in our society. The editorial points out that it is not an imported problem, since 70 per cent of the illiterate people in Canada were born here. Nor is it a problem of the elderly, since 40 per cent of the illiterate people are under the age of 45. Tragically, 60 per cent of the illiterate population is out of work. As Senator Fairbairn rightly said: "The illiterate population is our country's hidden shame."
With regard to my direct question of the Solicitor General, he assured me at the time that concrete steps would be taken shortly to deal with this situation. Indeed, on Wednesday of this week an adult basic education program will be launched in federal institutions across the country by the Correctional Service of Canada. Therefore, this is a good time to shed some more light on this unprecedented initiative, the success of which depends not only on my support or that of my colleagues in the House, but also on the awareness and goodwill of Canadians in general.
It would be instructive to begin with some further statistics. Currently, about one-half of all federal inmates have a level of competence below grade eight, which is considered to be the standard for conventional literacy. Out of these approximately 6,000 prisoners only 500, or less than 10 per cent, are enrolled in a basic education program, and of them only 150 or so will complete it successfully. Considering that 80 per cent of all prisoners are in jail for six years or less, this means that a great majority of those who enter being illiterate serve out their sentences and leave without any improvements. The question arises: Why educate prisoners? Some allege that this simply leads to well-informed, competent criminals. That is a narrowminded, vindictive view.
To begin with, criminals, even if they have at one time consciously violated the law, are human beings who at some point will return to society. To be able to function within society on par with other citizens certain basic skills are essential. Certainly, being able to read and write are in that category. Not having these skills is yet another obstacle for a productive return to those already branded with the social stigma of a "record".
The adjustment process is difficult enough as it is. No conclusive evidence exists linking crime and lack of education, but one may draw a common sense link between the latter and repeat offenders. After all, if there is one area in which prisoners are relatively well educated, it is crime. Therefore, it is reasonable to assume that lacking alternative "employment", many will again resort to crime. In 1979 the then Chief Justice of the U.S. Supreme Court expressed his concern in the following way:
In many of the institutions in this country today, a majority of the inmates cannot read or write. They are functional illiterates. This is why during the period of incarceration, a concentrated program must be available on two levels: first, to see to it that every prisoner learns to read and write; and, second, to see that each prisoner is trained in a marketable skill.
March 30, 1987

Aside from these specific considerations, it is important to look at what prisoners do during their term in a general way since, in a sense, that is their period of preparation for returning. These people have pride. But a lack of the most basic education often contributes to a low sense of self-esteem and self-confidence. Crime can be an escape from the system which may have failed them. Being better educated may enable them to discover new interests and skills and give their life in prison meaning and hope. Their preoccupation with anger and frustration may be channelled into something positive. Therefore, when they are released, literacy may qualify them to return, not just in a technical sense, but it should also raise their morale. Often, merely knowing that one can contribute in a meaningful way to society can be enormously inspiring and satisfying.
The goals of the program announced by the Solicitor General are ambitious. The target is to increase the number of successful completions of the program by 400 per cent in the first year, and ultimately to achieve a level of literacy among prisoners comparable to that of the Canadian public in general. This will not be easy, but the proposed initiative provides measures pointing in that direction. Incentives will be provided to encourage prisoners to participate. They will include linkage between program completion and, for instance, jobs in the institution and parole dates.
There will be improved co-ordination of the entire system so that prisoners transferred between jails will not be affected by the lack of standardized programs. More effort will be given to identify individual perceptual and hearing deficiencies, and correct them. Increased participation by qualified inmate tutors, with whom the prisoners will feel more comfortable, will also be encouraged.
In the entire process, success will depend largely upon the involvement of sectors of the community. Fortunately, a number of private organizations are ready and willing to help. For instance, there is Listen for Pleasure, a commercial group which distributes literacy programs in the form of cassettes- something that may be ideal for inmates often uneasy about formal classroom instruction. Frontier College is an institution whose basic mandate is to provide literacy in general, but its commitment to prisoners is very strong and well known.
And last, but most important, there are volunteer organizations, such as the John Howard Society and the Salvation Army, which have helped thousand of prisoners, and which try to foster goodwill toward them on the part of the public at large.
These groups provide an invaluable service, especially to young offenders and first-time offenders, during all stages, from court appearances, prison visits, and the problems associated with re-entry into society, to rebuilding family life, and in finding worthwhile employment.
Adjournment Debate
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I should like to emphasize the importance of recognizing inmates as decent human beings, with dreams of a better future. Yes, they have violated our social and criminal codes of conduct. However, given that ultimately they will rejoin society, they deserve every opportunity to be able to make a productive contribution and to shoulder some of society's responsibilities.

speakeroldname: Mr. Frangois Gerin (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want first of all to thank the Hon. Member for Don Valley-East (Mr. Attewell) for providing us with an opportunity to raise this important issue in the House, and to emphasize that the Solicitor General of Canada (Mr. Kelleher) shares his opinion on most of the points he has made. The Solicitor General of Canada, who is responsible for the penitentiary services in this country, is also well aware of the serious problem resulting from prisoners' illiteracy. His response, therefore, was to announce recently an adult basic training program which will be implemented in all Canadian prisons.
To give you an idea of the scope of the problem, I will give you some statistics: recently, in Canada, almost 50 per cent of the inmate population, which means about 6,000 individuals, were functionally illiterate. Out of an inmate population of 12,500 people, only 500 were enrolled in basic education programs, and each year barely 150 complete successfully the program they have started. With this initiative, the Solicitor General seeks to raise the level of literacy among inmates to a level similar to the one found in the general Canadian population, that is 70 to 80 per cent of people with a grade nine education or better. To reach that goal, we are aiming for a 400 per cent increase in the number of literate inmates in 1987-88, thus helping 600 more men and women to reach a grade nine education level. The second year the program budget will be doubled and the number should reach 1,200.
Why all these efforts, Mr. Speaker? Because illiteracy is a social and economic problem particularly acute among prisoners. Most of them, when they come out, are confronted with serious adjustment problems in their job or social life. Illiteracy is another obstacle to their social rehabilitation. Illiterate people cannot read or complete a job application; they cannot go through the classified ads to look for a job or a phone number; they cannot read the street signs or find an address. Such simple tasks can be beyond their ability. As to those who finally find a job, they cannot read instructions, regulations or safety precautions at the work site.
Mr. Speaker, the facts speak for themselves: chances of finding and keeping a job are better if the applicant can read and write. It has also been acknowledged that there is a direct correlation between the ability to keep a job and not to commit a subsequent offence. In light of that principle, whenever the National Parole Board examines the record of an inmate it takes into account the efforts he may have made to acquire a basic training.

March 30, 1987
Adjournment Debate
Other efforts will be made to encourage these people to take part in the program. As can readily be seen, the program is not additional punishment for the inmates, quite the contrary, it was designed to help them help themselves.
Mr. Speaker, the Solicitor General is convinced that most Canadians support him. According to a 1984 Gallup poll, more than 50 per cent of respondents felt that reading and writing should be the number one priority of programs for inmates. It is one way of expressing a basic truth concerning social reintegration: the inmate must have skills which will enable him to do something other than returning to criminal activities, and he can acquire the necessary skills by becoming more proficient at reading and writing. All Canadians who are concerned by this question will surely welcome this initiative whose aim is to enable inmates to reach that objective.

subtopic: THE ECONOMY-WESTERN ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT. (B) MANDATE OF ALLEGED OFFICE
THE ECONOMY-WESTERN ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT. (B) MANDATE OF ALLEGED OFFICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this evening I want to elaborate on why I want the federal Government to announce its plans for the Western Diversification Office. About a month or so ago I asked a question in the House about the western initiative office. At that time the Deputy Prime Minister and President of the Privy Council (Mr. Mazankowski) said that it did not exist.
Since that time they have changed the name of the office to the Western Diversification Office. Once again the Deputy Prime Minister refused to acknowledge that such an office existed. I do not know why they are delaying making an announcement because there is such an office in the bureaucracy now.
I have a copy of a leaked list of the employees of the Western Diversification Office. It was sent to me in a brown paper envelope. It is not a "Lome Nystrom" or an NDP list. It comes out of the Public Service of Canada from someone who is in the knowledge, in the situation, and has access to the list of employees of the Western Diversification Office.
It is an office which has not yet been announced by the federal Government. It is an office which does not have a budget of which we know or a mandate of which we know. It is an office which does not have the discretionary power to decide on what projects will be accepted or not or what projects will be funded or not. Yet, there is such an office.
I want to read into the record and make an announcement on behalf of the federal Government. On behalf of the Deputy Prime Minister I announce that there is a Western Diversification Office. It is located on the fourth floor at 435 Ellice Avenue in Winnipeg, Manitoba, in the Canadian Institute of Industrial Technology Building. This is a National Research building in Winnipeg.
When I first mentioned it, the Deputy Prime Minister said that these 15 employees were employees of the Minister of State for Science and Technology (Mr. Oberle). That is not true, and I will read into the record the names of the employees.
First, there are two co-chairpersons. The first is John Blackwood, Co-Chairperson of Resource Industries. He is located in Room No. 473 and his phone number is 949-6956. The other Co-Chairperson, Mr. Speaker-and do not forget that the Deputy Prime Minister said that this office did not exist-is Mr. Anthony Reynolds. He is co-chairperson of Manufacturing and Service. His Room No. is 474. His phone number is 949-6589. These are the two co-chairpersons.
In addition, the Western Diversification Office, which has not been announced by the Government of Canada, has a secretary. The secretary's name is Kay Hoare in Room 472. In addition, there is a senior policy adviser for Manufacturing and Services. This person's name is Robert Stalker. In addition, there is Derryl Millar, Senior Policy Adviser for Resource Industries. There is also Burt Waslander, Senior Economic Adviser. By the way, he was a person in the Ottawa headquarters of DRIE, the Department of Regional Industrial Expansion. He is now in Winnipeg in Room No. 466.
There is John Inns, Senior Project Manager. There is Gary Hosea, Co-ordinator of High Technology. There is Randy Winnitowy, Co-ordinator of Resource Processing. By the way, Mr. Winnitowy is from my home province. He comes from the Saskatoon office of DRIE.
There is also Bill Whiting, Co-ordinator of Traditional Industries. There is Kim Nishikaze, Communications Officer. There is Terry Gibson, who is Project Manager of Resource Industries; Mr. Ron Smith, Administration Co-ordinator; Janice Dyck, a word processing operator; and Joann Primrose, who is a secretary.
In addition, this Western Diversification Office, which does not exist according to the Deputy Prime Minister, has a communications centre. That communications centre is located in Room No. 461. In case you want to communicate with them, Mr. Speaker, their phone number is 949-2489. If that is busy, you can call 949-7950. That is the Western Diversification Office. It has not been announced by the Government of Canada. It is in existence. It is doing some work. It is paying rent at the NRC building in Winnipeg which happens to be in the riding of my friend, the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Keeper). I want to know now from the Parliamentary Secretary, who is a very honest, decent forthright gentleman from Alberta, why the secrecy. Why has the federal Government not announced that the office exists? Why has the Government not told us what the mandate of the office is and whether or not there will be a budget?
I have another bit of information that you will be interested in, Mr. Speaker. I have been told by a reliable source, who I
March 30, 1987

cannot name, that the federal Government did not make this announcement because it is planning a very slick, audio-visual presentation in the four western provinces in order to kick it off at an opportune political time, using senior Ministers from each of the four provinces. Winnipeg, of course, is the headquarters, so I assume the Minister involved in Manitoba would be someone like the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp), in Saskatchewan it would be one of our two Ministers, in Alberta I would assume it would be the Deputy Prime Minister and in British Columbia one of the Ministers from there. Is the Government going to use taxpayers money for a slick, political kick-off rather than do some real work on western diversification?
With regard to western diversification, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) does say that there is work going on. The work is in his office and there will be an announcement very soon. Up to now there has been nothing at all in terms of western diversification. What we have had so far are western emergency programs. We appreciate them, like the $1 billion for farmers, the ending of the PGRT and the $350 million to western oil and gas. But that is not western diversification. That is western emergency aid which does not diversify the economy.
What we need in western Canada is a western Canadian economic strategy to diversify the economy, one with more local control, more self-reliance, more local input where western Canadians have more say. That is what I want and that is what western Canadians want. I hope that this office will have some input in real industrial economic strategy for western Canada so that in the future we will have a more balanced view of what the national interest is. I do not want to see more CF-18 decisions made that do not diversify the western Canadian economy but instead restrict the possibilities for diversification.
1 look forward to my friend from Alberta enlightening this House since the Deputy Prime Minister felt he could not do so.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jack Shields (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: THE ECONOMY-WESTERN ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT. (B) MANDATE OF ALLEGED OFFICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to reply to the statements by the Hon. Member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom). First I want to compliment and thank him for supporting the Progressive Conservative Government on its western Canadian strategy.
I want to point out that this matter is not secret. We are not preparing a slick, audio-visual presentation. I am sorry to say that the Hon. Member for Yorkton-Melville was again using innuendo in this House in an attempt to discredit the Government.
He talks about the brown paper envelope with this list of people working in an office in Winnipeg. He says it came from
Adjournment Debate
someone who knows who has access to the information. He admits that he does not know from where the envelope came but in it there is a list of people who are in a so-called secret office.
I would like to point out that the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion (Mr. Cote) has asked officials of his Department to undertake wide-ranging analytical work on the manufacturing and service industries of Canada. This work, of course, and I think the Hon. Member should agree, illustrates again the high priority which the Government places on western diversification. For administration convenience, the work is being co-ordinated by the Winnipeg office of the Department of Regional Industrial Expansion. The officers involved could not be accommodated in DRIEs permanent offices, so temporary accommodation has been rented in the Canadian Institute of Industrial Technology Building.
I underline that that is not the Western Diversification Office in Winnipeg. There is no Western Diversification Office in Winnipeg. The Hon. Member knows exactly what we are talking about. He heard the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Mazankowski) say there is no Western Diversification Office in Winnipeg. There is an office of the Department of Regional Industrial Expansion. Employees of the Department are doing analytical work so this Government can make decisions based on a good study of what is going on in western Canada. For some reason the Hon. Member would rather believe something from a brown envelope. Of course, the NDP are very used to brown paper envelopes.

speechtext: So are the Tories.
